title: Lagana: Clean Monday sesame bread
ingredients:
1 × 7g sachet of fast-action dried yeast
1 tablespoon caster sugar
500g strong white bread flour, plus extra for dusting
¾ teaspoon fine sea salt, plus extra for sprinkling
2 tablespoons olive oil, plus extra for greasing
3 tablespoons sesame seeds
steps:
Place the yeast in a measuring jug with half of the caster sugar and top up with 275ml of warm water. Leave to one side for 5 minutes. Place the bread flour in a large mixing bowl, whisk in the sea salt and make a well in the centre. Pour in the yeast water and olive oil and mix into the flour with a fork until it all comes together – add more water if needed; you want a moist dough, not too dry, as it will dry out a little during kneading and proving. Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 10 minutes, until it is smooth and elastic. If you have a free-standing mixer with a dough hook, do it in that by all means. Transfer the dough to a clean, oiled bowl, cover with a tea towel and leave somewhere warm for 1–1½ hours, to double in size.
When the dough is ready, turn it out onto a lightly floured surface and knock out the air. Lightly oil a large baking or roasting tray, about 30 × 25cm, and stretch the dough in to fit the tin (you can roll with a rolling pin or use your hands). Cover and leave to one side for a second prove to double in size, around 20 minutes.
Meanwhile preheat your oven to 220°C/fan 200°C/gas mark 7. Boil a kettle. When the dough has doubled in size, dissolve the remaining caster sugar in two tablespoons of boiling water. Gently press the dough all over with your fingertips to make little indents all over the surface, then brush with the sugar water. Sprinkle over the sesame seeds and a good pinch of sea salt. Place the tray in the oven and bake for about 20–22 minutes, until golden and crunchy on the outside, and cooked through. Serve in thin slices alongside other Clean Monday favourites.
source: The Secret to Delicious Vegan Cooking from the Mediterranean and Beyond.epub

title: Little za’atar buns
ingredients:
1 tablespoon caster sugar
1 × 7g sachet of fast-action dried yeast
500g strong white bread flour, plus extra for dusting
¾ teaspoon fine sea salt
125ml extra virgin olive oil, plus extra for greasing
6 tablespoons za’atar
½ teaspoon pul biber
steps:
Add the sugar and yeast to a jug and whisk in 275ml of warm water then leave to one side for a couple of minutes. Place the flour in a large mixing bowl and whisk in the salt, then make a well in the centre. Mix in the yeast water and 25ml of the extra virgin olive oil until well combined – add more water if needed; you want a moist dough, it shouldn’t be too dry. Transfer the dough to a flour-dusted surface and knead for around 8–10 minutes, until smooth and elastic. Wash and dry the mixing bowl, then lightly oil it. Return it to the bowl, drizzle with a little more oil and leave to prove for around 1–1½ hours (this will depend on how warm your kitchen is), until doubled in size.
When the dough has risen, turn it out onto a clean surface, knock it back and roll into a rectangle about 26 × 40cm. Brush over a layer of olive oil and evenly sprinkle over the za’atar and pul biber, leaving a 1cm border around the edges. Pat the spice mixture gently into the dough with the back of a tablespoon. Starting with a short side, roll the dough up as tightly as you can. Trim off the uneven excess bits at the end. Slice the dough into 9 pieces. Pour enough oil to just cover the base of a 23cm square cake tin and pop in the slices, swirl facing up. Cover and leave to one side for a second prove to double in size, about 30 minutes.
Meanwhile, preheat the oven to 200°C/fan 180°C/gas mark 6. When the buns have roughly doubled in size, bake for 25–30 minutes, until golden. As soon as they come out of the oven, drizzle over the remaining olive oil and leave to absorb in the tin for 10 minutes before serving.

title: Covrigi: salty poppy seed twists
ingredients:
1 tablespoon caster sugar
1 × 7g sachet of fast-action dried yeast
500g strong white bread flour, plus extra for dusting
1 teaspoon fine sea salt
3 tablespoons olive or sunflower oil
2 tablespoons bicarbonate of soda
1 tablespoon poppy seeds
1 tablespoon sesame seeds
¾ teaspoon flaky sea salt
1 tablespoon onion flakes
steps:
Place the caster sugar in a measuring jug with the yeast and stir in 260ml of warm water. Whisk and leave to one side for 5 minutes. Place the flour in a large mixing bowl and whisk in the fine sea salt. Make a well in the centre, and whisk the yeast water into the flour with a fork. Add two tablespoons of the oil and bring the dough together. Turn it out onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 5 –10 minutes, until the dough is smooth and elastic. Transfer to a lightly greased clean bowl and leave to prove for 1–1½ hours, or until doubled in size.
When the dough is ready, turn it out onto your work top and knock out the air. Divide into eight even-sized pieces. For a traditional pretzel shape, roll each piece into a 50cm long sausage. Fold the ends into the centre, crossing them over to create a heart shape, and pinch them in place. For the twirled shape, cut a piece of the dough in half and roll both pieces into a 35cm long sausage. Pinch the ends together and twist the strips, then join the ends together to create a ring. Transfer to two lightly oiled baking sheets and leave to prove until doubled in size, about 20 minutes.
Preheat your oven to 220°C/fan 200°C/gas mark 7. Bring a large pan of water to the boil and add the bicarbonate of soda to the water. In a bowl, mix together the poppy seeds, sesame seeds, flaky sea salt and onion flakes. Using a large mesh strainer, submerge the pretzels into the water for 30 seconds, then let the moisture dry off them and return them to their trays. When they are all done, brush with the remaining olive or sunflower oil and sprinkle liberally with the spice mix – patting it in place. Bake in the oven for around 18–20 minutes, until deeply golden brown but still fluffy in the middle. Leave to one side to cool (if you can wait).

title: Koulouri: Cypriot village bread
ingredients:
1 × 7g sachet of fast-action dried yeast
1½ tablespoons caster sugar
1 piece of mastic
2 pieces of mehlepi
500g strong white bread flour, plus extra for dusting
1 teaspoon fine sea salt
¼ teaspoon ground cinnamon
2 tablespoons olive oil, plus extra for greasing
4 tablespoons sesame seeds
2 teaspoons nigella seeds
½ teaspoon aniseed
steps:
Pour 330ml of warm water into a measuring jug and whisk in the yeast and a tablespoon of the caster sugar. Leave to one side for a couple of minutes. Meanwhile, grind the mastic and then mehlepi separately, each with a teaspoon of flour until finely ground. Place the rest of the flour (minus one tablespoon) with the sea salt, ground cinnamon, ground mastic and ground mehlepi into a large mixing bowl and whisk together. Make a well in the centre, pour in the yeast water, along with the olive oil, and whisk it with a fork. You may need to add a further two or three tablespoons of water at this point if your dough isn’t coming together. It’s better to have a slightly wetter dough, rather than too dry. When it has all come together, turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and knead it for 10 minutes. Try not to over-flour the surface or dough, as it will become more elastic as you work it. Transfer the kneaded dough to a clean, lightly oiled bowl, cover with a clean tea towel and leave in a warm place to prove. It will take 1–1½ hours to double in size.
When the dough is ready, turn it out onto a clean surface and knock it back. Roll it into a long sausage, around 30cm, and place it diagonally on an oiled baking sheet. Using a sharp knife or dough cutter, cut the dough into 10 pieces, and very gently pull them apart so there is a 2mm gap between each piece. Whisk the reserved tablespoon of flour with two tablespoons of warm water to create a loose paste and brush the dough all over. Mix the sesame seeds in a bowl with the nigella seeds and aniseed and pat all over the dough – it may look like a lot, but you want a really even crust, with some underneath too if you can. Cover with a tea towel and prove again until doubled in size, about 30 minutes.
Preheat your oven to 220°C/fan 200°C/gas mark 7. Boil a kettle. Pour 150ml of boiling water in a small ovenproof dish. When you place the bread in the oven, place the dish at the bottom also. Leave in the oven for at least 22–25 minutes before checking. It should be golden brown all over. Leave to cool for at least 10 minutes, before tucking in.

title: Fatayer muhammara: smoky red pepper and walnut flatbreads
ingredients:
1 tablespoon caster sugar
1 × 7g sachet of fast-action dried yeast
350g strong white bread flour, plus extra for dusting
½ teaspoon fine sea salt
4 tablespoons olive oil, plus extra for greasing
½ × batch of muhammara
1 pomegranate
½ bunch of flat-leaf parsley
A few mint sprigs
4 tablespoons pomegranate molasses
steps:
Place the caster sugar and yeast in a jug then stir in 200ml of warm water and leave to one side for a few minutes. Lightly oil a mixing bowl and a couple of baking trays. In another large mixing bowl whisk together the flour and sea salt and make a well in the middle. Pour in the yeast water and two tablespoons of the olive oil and mix it in with a fork so it comes together, adding a little more water if it feels too dry. Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 10 minutes, until smooth and elastic. Transfer it to a clean, lightly oiled bowl, and leave to prove for 1–1½ hours, or until the dough has doubled in size.
Meanwhile, make the muhammara as instructed here . When the dough is ready, knock out the air and roll into a sausage. Cut the dough into 8 pieces and roll each piece out into a circle, around 12cm. Lay the circles out on the lightly greased baking trays and top each with a heaped tablespoon of muhammara. Spread the muhammara out into a thin layer, leaving a 1cm border around the edge. Leave to prove again for 20 minutes.
Meanwhile, preheat your oven to 220°C/fan 200°C/gas mark 7. Drizzle each flatbread with a little oil. Bake in the oven for 18–20 minutes, or until golden and cooked through. While they are baking, carefully pick the pomegranate seeds. Pick and roughly chop the parsley and mint leaves. When the flatbreads are ready, drizzle with the pomegranate molasses, sprinkle over the pomegranate seeds and chopped herbs and serve warm.

title: Bobalki: Christmas dough balls, two ways
ingredients:
1 × 7g sachet of fast-action dried yeast
1 tablespoon caster sugar
500g strong white bread flour, plus extra for dusting
¾ teaspoon fine sea salt
3 tablespoons olive oil, plus extra for greasing
3 onions
3 tbsp olive oil
1 heaped teaspoon caraway seeds
150g sauerkraut
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
3 tablespoons poppy seeds
1 lemon
150ml honey (see introduction)
steps:
Place the yeast in a measuring jug with the caster sugar and whisk in 275ml of warm water. Leave to one side for 5 minutes. Place the flour in a large mixing bowl, whisk in the sea salt and make a well in the centre. Pour in the yeast water and olive oil and mix in with a fork until it all comes together. Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 10 minutes, until it is smooth and elastic. If you have a free-standing mixer with a dough hook, you can use that if you prefer. Transfer the dough to a clean, lightly oiled bowl, cover with a tea towel and leave somewhere warm for 1–1½ hours, until double in size.
Lightly oil a large roasting tray; if you don’t have a very large one, oil a couple. When the dough is ready, turn it out onto a lightly floured surface and knock out the air. Roll the dough out to a 2.5cm-thick sausage and cut into small, even pieces, so that when you roll them they’re balls about 2.5cm. Place them all on a lightly oiled baking tray, so they are all just touching. Cover and leave to one side for a second prove to double in size, about 30 minutes.
Meanwhile, preheat your oven to 220°C/fan 200°C/gas mark 7. When the dough balls have roughly doubled in size, bake for 18–20 minutes, or until golden and cooked through. Remove from the oven and leave to cool before combining with one of the two toppings.
For the sauerkraut, onion and caraway bobalki: Peel and finely chop the onions. Place a medium frying pan on medium-low and pour in the olive oil. Add the chopped onions and caraway seeds and season generously with salt and pepper. Sauté for 12–15 minutes, until soft and lightly browned. Drain and chop the sauerkraut and add to the pan. Turn the heat up a little and fry for a further 3 minutes, until golden.
When ready, break the dough balls apart and place in a large colander directly in the sink. Boil your kettle and pour enough just-boiled water over the balls to soften them slightly, but not turn them mushy (you can do this in batches if easier). Drain the balls and place in a large mixing bowl or tray and spoon over the sauerkraut mixture. Toss together well.
For the honey, lemon and poppy seed bobalki: Place the poppy seeds in a mortar and finely grate in the lemon zest. Grind just enough with a pestle so they release their flavours but retain a good seedy texture, and keep to one side. Pour the honey into a small saucepan and squeeze in the juice of half the lemon. Warm over a medium heat.
When ready, break the dough balls apart and place in a large colander directly in the sink. Boil your kettle and pour enough just-boiled water over the balls to soften them slightly, but not turn them mushy (you can do this in batches). Drain the balls and place in a large mixing bowl or tray and pour over the warm lemony honey. Sprinkle over the ground poppy seeds and toss with your hands to coat the bread completely.
Serve the bobalki straight away, or chill until needed.

title: Eliopites: olive, mint and coriander buns
ingredients:
175g pitted black olives
2 onions
4 mint sprigs
½ bunch of coriander
1 tablespoon caster sugar
1 × 7g sachet of fast-action dried yeast
500g strong white bread flour, plus extra for dusting
¾ teaspoon fine sea salt
100ml olive oil, plus extra for greasing
steps:
Tear the olives in half. Peel and finely chop the onions. Pick and finely slice the mint leaves. Finely slice the coriander leaves and stalks. Mix everything together and leave to one side. Mix the sugar and yeast in a jug with 225ml of warm water. In a large bowl whisk together the flour and salt and pour in the olive oil, rubbing it in with your fingers to create breadcrumbs. Slowly pour in the yeast water, mixing it in until you have a wet dough, adding more water if it feels a little dry. Knead it for a few minutes then add the herby olive and onion mixture and mix in. Turn it out onto a flour-dusted surface, and knead for 10 minutes until smooth. Return the dough to a clean, oiled bowl, cover with a tea towel and leave in a warm spot for around 1–1½ hours, or until doubled in size.
Once the dough is ready, turn it out onto a clean surface and knock out the air. Knead it for a further minute or two then divide the dough into 12 pieces and shape them into rolls. Place on an oiled baking tray, cover with a tea towel and leave to prove again for a further 30 minutes, or until doubled in size.
Meanwhile, preheat your oven to full whack. When the buns have doubled in size, bake for 20–25 minutes, turning the temperature down to 220°C/fan 200°C/gas mark 7 as soon as they go in. They are ready when they are golden brown, and cooked through. Leave to cool for at least 10 minutes before serving.

title: Koliva: sweet memorial offering
ingredients:
350g whole wheat grains
200g skin-on almonds (you can buy them blanched but this method means you end up splitting them in half too)
100g sesame seeds
250g sultanas
2 pomegranates
2 teaspoons aniseed
1 tablespoon ground cinnamon
Icing sugar, optional
Silver dragée decorations, optional
steps:
On the Friday night before you want to take this to be blessed, soak the whole wheat grains and almonds in separate bowls in plenty of cold water. Leave until the next day. Then when you are ready, place the wheat grains in a pan of fresh water over a high heat and bring to the boil, then reduce the heat and simmer for 30 minutes, or until the grains have cooked and start to split in half. Drain in a colander and then leave them to cool and dry. Line a tray with kitchen paper and spread the cooked wheat out so the paper fully absorbs any moisture. When the wheat is dry, transfer to a bowl, then discard damp kitchen paper and replace with new. Spread the wheat evenly out on the freshly lined tray, then place the tray, uncovered, in the fridge.
For the almonds, keep them in their bowl of water while you peel off or pop them out of their skins. This is quite time consuming but also therapeutic. Encourage them to split in half, also. Then, place the peeled halved almonds in a fresh bowl of cold water and in the fridge also. Place the sesame seeds in a small sieve and wash under cold running water. Place the sieve over a bowl and leave in the fridge to drain and dry. Wash the sultanas in a colander then leave to drain and dry in the sink. Spread them out on a kitchen paper-lined tray or plate and store in the fridge. (Greeks wash everything. I imagine this is to do with how things were stored in the old times. I don’t know if there is such a good reason to do it now, but I do it anyway.) Carefully remove the seeds from the pomegranates, discarding the pith and skin, and keep in a covered container in the fridge.
On the Sunday morning of the memorial, put together your koliva. You may want to keep some of the almonds, sesame seeds, pomegranate seeds and sultanas aside for decoration. Place the rest of them in a large bowl with the cooked wheat, aniseed and cinnamon and mix together well. Spoon onto an oval tray that has a lip all around the edge, and pat out evenly. You can then decorate how you wish – it is common to either spell out the initials of the person you are remembering, or mark a cross. You can adorn the koliva directly or coat it in icing sugar first; it is up to you.

title: Tahini, cinnamon and carob pancakes
ingredients:
250g plain flour
2 tablespoons caster sugar
½ teaspoon ground cinnamon
¼ teaspoon fine sea salt
500ml milk of your choice (oat and almond work well)
2 tablespoons olive or vegetable oil, plus extra for greasing
5 tablespoons tahini
3 tablespoons honey (or caster sugar)
2 tablespoons carob syrup
2 bananas, optional
steps:
Place the plain flour in a large mixing bowl and whisk in the caster sugar, the cinnamon and half the sea salt. Make a well in the middle and whisk in the milk and oil until smooth. It should be the consistency of double cream – if it is a little thick add a splash more milk. Leave the batter to rest in the fridge for half an hour if possible. Put a kettle on. In a small bowl, mix the tahini with three or four tablespoons of just-boiled water until smooth, then stir in the honey and the rest of the salt. Set aside.
When you are ready to make your pancakes, place a large non-stick frying pan on a medium heat. Drizzle in a touch of oil, and use kitchen paper to spread it over the pan. You don’t want too much oil, just enough to cover the base. When the pan is hot, ladle in the batter and tilt the pan so it covers the base. The first pancake often goes a bit wrong – chef’s perks for snacking – but it will help you figure out how much batter you need to cover your pan. Cook for a few minutes until lightly golden underneath, then flip over. Because there is no egg in the mixture, they don’t quite brown the way regular pancakes do, but you will know when they are ready. Cook for a further minute or two, then serve or transfer to a plate. You can either serve the pancakes as you go, drizzling them with the sweetened tahini and then the carob syrup on top, or cook all the batter and keep them warm on a plate in a low oven. Repeat with all the batter, rubbing a little oil on the base of the pan every so often. If you’ve kept the pancakes warm as you’ve cooked them, arrange them on a platter and, when ready, drizzle the tahini and carob over the lot. I like them with sliced banana – I think it works well with the nutty sweet tahini and rich carob, but that is up to you.

title: Ful medames: creamy, spiced fava beans
ingredients:
250g dried split fava beans, or 2 × 400g tins of cooked beans (if fava beans are hard to come by, you can use cannellini, haricot or borlotti beans)
1 onion
3 garlic cloves
Extra virgin olive oil
½ teaspoon ground cumin
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 large green chilli
½ bunch of flat-leaf parsley
1–2 lemons
2 ripe tomatoes
steps:
If you are making this from scratch, wash the dried fava beans, discard any stones, and leave to soak overnight in plenty of cold water. Then when you are ready to cook them, place in a pan with 5 times as much fresh cold water and bring to a boil. Reduce the heat, and simmer gently for 2 hours, or until tender and cooked through. Check them occasionally to make sure they haven’t boiled dry. Drain the cooked beans but reserve a large mug of the cooking water.
If you’re using tinned beans, start here: drain them and reserve the liquid.
Peel and finely chop the onion and garlic. Place a large frying pan on a medium-low heat. Add two tablespoons of olive oil, the chopped onion and half the chopped garlic; sauté for 10 minutes till the onions are soft but not coloured. Stir in the cumin then add the drained fava plus about 200ml of the cooking/tin water. Bring to the boil, season, then reduce the heat to low for around 10 minutes. Towards the end of cooking, especially if you’re using tinned beans, you might need to use a potato masher to gently mash the beans. You don’t want a purée, just a creamy broken consistency – you can add a little more liquid here if need be.
While the beans are cooking, make the dressing. Halve and finely chop the chilli (for a milder dressing you can remove the seeds) and place in a mortar with the remaining garlic and a good pinch of salt. Bash with the pestle until broken down, smoother and well combined. Roughly chop the parsley, then add that to the mortar and pound it in. Halve one lemon and squeeze in its juice, then stir in a couple of tablespoons of oil to loosen to your taste. Halve and deseed the tomatoes, and finely chop the flesh.
Serve the creamy fava beans drizzled with the spicy green dressing over the top and scattered with the chopped tomatoes. Cut the remaining lemon into wedges and serve on the side. Perfect with warm pita bread, sticks of cucumber, chopped spring onions and olives.
source: The Secret to Delicious Vegan Cooking from the Mediterranean and Beyond.epub

title: Balila: crushed garlicky chickpeas with asparagus
ingredients:
500g cooked chickpeas , or 2 × 400g jars/tins of chickpeas
4 garlic cloves
250g asparagus
4 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil, plus extra for drizzling
1 teaspoon ground cumin
½ lemon
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
½ bunch of flat-leaf parsley
steps:
If cooking your own chickpeas, get those ready and keep to one side, along with the cooking liquid.
Peel and finely chop the garlic. Snap the woody ends off the asparagus stalks and discard them. Finely slice the stalks – I like to keep the tips whole and sliced in half lengthways. Place the olive oil in a medium saucepan over a medium-low heat and add the garlic and asparagus. Fry the vegetables for 5 minutes, then add the ground cumin. Fry for 2 minutes, then add chickpeas and 200ml of the cooking water. If you are using tinned chickpeas, just add the liquid from the tins. Increase the heat to high and bring to the boil, and use the back of a fork to crush about a third of the chickpeas and make the mixture a little creamy. Reduce the heat to medium and simmer for 10 minutes. Squeeze in the juice from the lemon half, season generously and continue to cook for 5 more minutes. Meanwhile, finely chop the parsley. When the chickpeas look creamy and thick, the balila is ready. Taste and adjust the seasoning as needed, then spoon into a serving dish. Finish by drizzling with extra virgin olive oil and scattering over the chopped parsley. This can be served warm or at room temperature.

title: Pisiseeh: saut é ed bread in garlic oil
ingredients:
4 garlic cloves
2 stale large pita breads, or ½ stale Turkish pide
4 tablespoons olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 tablespoon dukkah , optional
A few pinches of pul biber or dried chilli flakes, optional
steps: Peel and finely chop the garlic. Tear the stale pita or pide into small, bite-sized pieces. Boil a kettle of water so you have hot water ready to go. Place the olive oil in a medium saucepan over a low heat and add the chopped garlic. Fry for a minute or two; it shouldn’t go crispy, you want it just cooked enough to infuse the oil and start to turn golden, then stir in the torn bread. Turn the heat up a little and fry the bread for a minute, stirring to coat in the garlicky oil. Slowly add 250ml of the boiled water, stir until absorbed, and add a further 100–200ml of water, so the bread is soft but not too soupy. Season generously with salt and black pepper, and finish with the dukkah and a pinch of pul biber or dried chilli flakes, if you like.

title: Makdous: baby aubergines with walnuts and chilli
ingredients:
5 garlic cloves
1 red chilli
1 red pepper
Olive oil
1 × 400g tin of chopped tomatoes
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 tablespoon red wine vinegar
125g walnuts
½ bunch of coriander
½ teaspoon dried chilli flakes
½ teaspoon ground cinnamon
½ teaspoon ground cumin
½ teaspoon ground coriander
10 baby aubergines
steps:
Peel the garlic cloves, and finely slice two of them. Halve the chilli, remove the seeds and finely slice. Halve the pepper, remove the seeds and chop into 1cm pieces. Pour two tablespoons of olive oil into a medium saucepan and place over a medium-low heat. Add the sliced garlic and fry for a couple of minutes, then add half the sliced chilli and all the chopped pepper. Sauté for 10 minutes, then stir in the tin of chopped tomatoes and season well. Fill the tin with water, add to the pan and bring to the boil. When it starts to bubble, reduce the heat and stir in the vinegar. Simmer for 15 minutes, until the sauce has thickened a little.
While the sauce is simmering, make the aubergine stuffing. Place the three remaining garlic cloves into a food processor along with the walnuts. Cut off the coriander stalks and add them to the food processor, reserving the leaves. Add the dried chilli flakes, ground cinnamon, ground cumin and ground coriander and season well. Blitz everything together until finely chopped then add just enough olive oil to bring the mixture together. Leaving the stalks intact, slice the aubergines in half lengthways twice, so that it is in quarters, but is still connected by the stalk. Stuff the inside of the aubergines with the walnut mixture, a couple of teaspoons in each. This is easiest done with your hands to compress the nuts inside. Reserve any remaining mixture for the sauce.
Place a large frying pan on a medium-low heat and add four tablespoons of olive oil. Gently lay in the aubergines and fry for 8–10 minutes, until softened on one side, then turn them over and fry on the other side for 5 minutes. At this stage you can either carefully remove the aubergines to a plate, spoon the pepper-tomato sauce into the frying pan and place the aubergines on the sauce. Or you can spoon the sauce around the aubergines, nestling them in. Dot in any remaining walnut mixture, cover the pan with a lid and simmer for 15 minutes, by which point the aubergines should be tender. Roughly chop the reserved coriander leaves and scatter over the top before serving.

title: Fattet houmous
ingredients:
1 × quantity of houmous , or about 600g good-quality shop-bought houmous
4 pita breads
Olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
50g pine nuts
70g tahini
1 lemon
2 garlic cloves
½ bunch of flat-leaf parsley
1 green chilli
100g radishes
½ pomegranate
2 tablespoons pomegranate molasses
½ teaspoon sumac
steps:
Make the houmous as instructed here , and if you’re cooking the chickpeas from scratch, reserve 125ml of the cooking water.
Preheat your oven to 180°C/fan 160°C/gas mark 4. Cut the pita bread into 2.5cm squares and lay out on a baking tray. Drizzle the bread with a little olive oil and season with salt and pepper. Scatter the pine nuts into a small baking dish and place it and the baking tray in the oven. Remove the pine nuts after 7 minutes, when golden, and bake the pita squares for a further 8 minutes, until they are golden also.
Meanwhile, spoon the tahini into a large mixing bowl and juice the lemon. Boil a kettle. Stir the lemon juice and 100ml boiling water into the tahini (add an additional few tablespoons if it is quite thick; it should have the consistency of double cream). Peel the garlic cloves then finely grate them straight into the bowl, and season generously. Whisk together and taste, adjusting the seasoning as needed. Finely chop the parsley leaves and stalks. Halve, deseed and finely slice the chilli. Trim and finely slice the radishes. Pick the pomegranate seeds and keep to one side.
To assemble the fattet houmous, toss the toasted pita with the reserved 125ml of chickpea water (alternatively, you can use boiling water) and spread two-thirds of it into a large serving dish. Spoon over the houmous, then scatter over the remaining pita squares and half of the radishes. Drizzle over the tahini dressing. Scatter over the remaining radishes and drizzle with the pomegranate molasses. Garnish with the chopped parsley, the pomegranate seeds, sumac and sliced chilli. Serve straight away, with fresh bread for mopping up all the dressing.

title: Galayet bandora: fried tomatoes
ingredients:
1kg ripe tomatoes
2 onions
3 garlic cloves
4 tablespoons olive oil
2 green chillies
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
steps:
Peel the tomatoes and then roughly each one, discarding the core but keeping the seeds. Peel and finely chop the onions and garlic cloves. Place the olive oil in a wide saucepan or large frying pan over a low heat. Add the chopped onion and garlic and fry for 10 minutes, until soft and translucent. For a gentle chilli heat, pierce the two chillies all over with the tip of your knife and add them to the pan, along with the tomatoes. If you like it fiery, deseed then finely chop one or both chillies before adding them and the tomatoes to the pan. Season well and turn the heat up a little. Fry for 15–20 minutes, stirring often, until the tomatoes have softened and thickened and juice has reduced.
When the tomatoes are almost ready, pick and finely chop the parsley and mint leaves. Toast the bread or pita, if you like, and drizzle with extra virgin olive oil. Sprinkle the herbs over the top of the tomatoes, and serve with the bread on the side.
source: The Secret to Delicious Vegan Cooking from the Mediterranean and Beyond.epub

title: Broad bean, dill and tomato salad
ingredients:
1.5kg broad beans (350–400g podded weight)
4 spring onions
1 lemon
3 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 bunch of dill
3 ripe tomatoes
½ garlic clove
steps:
Pod the broad beans. Bring a pan of water to the boil and blanch the beans for 2½–3 minutes, depending on their size. Drain and immediately transfer to a bowl of ice water. Leave them for 5 minutes, then remove the opaque skins, so that you are just left with the vibrant green beans inside. Trim and finely slice the spring onions and toss through the broad beans, along with the juice of the lemon, and two tablespoons of the extra virgin olive oil and a generous pinch each of sea salt and freshly ground black pepper. Finely chop the dill and stir through. Check the seasoning and leave to one side.
Place a box grater in a large shallow bowl and grate in the flesh and seeds of the tomatoes on the coarsest side; discard the skins. Finely grate in the peeled garlic clove, then stir in the final tablespoon of extra virgin olive oil and season to taste. When the dressing is ready, pile the dressed broad beans on top of the grated tomatoes and serve with fresh bread.

title: Roast tomato, orzo and rocket salad with roasted garlic dressing
ingredients:
750g ripe tomatoes – a mixture of sizes and types
4 garlic cloves
Olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
½ tablespoon dried oregano
75g pine nuts
250g orzo
2 tablespoons red wine vinegar
1 heaped teaspoon Dijon mustard
3 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil
1 bunch of basil (use Greek basil if you have access to it)
50g wild rocket
steps:
Preheat your oven to 170°C/fan 150°C/gas mark 3½. Chop the tomatoes: halve any smaller ones and cut any larger ones into quarters. Lay them out in a roasting tray, cut side up, dot in the unpeeled garlic and drizzle with olive oil. Season with salt and pepper and scatter over the oregano. Place the tray in the oven and slowly cook the tomatoes for 1–1½ hours, so they cook down and become jammy – but not completely dried out. Scatter the pine nuts in a smaller tray and add to the oven for the last 12 minutes of cooking, just to toast them slightly.
While the tomatoes are cooling, cook the orzo. Place a large pan of salted water on to boil, cook the pasta according to the packet instructions until just cooked through, then drain, reserving a mug of the hot, starchy pasta water. Rinse the pasta in a fine colander or sieve under cold running water, to stop it overcooking and cool it quickly, then drain and transfer to a large mixing bowl.
To make the dressing, carefully remove the garlic from the tomato tray and pop the flesh from the skins. Place the garlic flesh in a mixing bowl, then use the back of a fork to mash the soft garlic with a pinch of salt and the red wine vinegar. Once they are smooth, whisk in the mustard, extra virgin olive oil and add a generous couple of pinches of pepper. Toss the dressing into the pasta along with the cooked, cooled tomatoes and toasted pine nuts.. If it doesn’t quite feel loose enough, add a splash of pasta water. Tear in all the basil leaves, add the rocket and mix together well. Serve straight away or keep in the fridge until needed. If you are making ahead of time, leave the torn basil leaves and rocket in a layer on top of the dressed pasta and mix together at the last minute.

title: Pomegranate fattoush
ingredients:
2 pita breads
Extra virgin olive oil
1 teaspoon dried oregano
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 tablespoon pomegranate molasses
1 lemon
1 garlic clove
½ pomegranate
500g ripe, mixed-colour tomatoes
1 small or ½ large cucumber
6 spring onions
1 bunch of flat-leaf parsley
6 radishes
1 cos lettuce or 2 little gem lettuces
1 teaspoon sumac
steps:
Preheat the oven to 180°C/fan 160°C/gas mark 4. Open out the pita breads like a book and drizzle with olive oil, sprinkle over the oregano and season a little. Pop in the oven for 12–15 minutes until lightly golden and crisp. Leave to cool for 10 minutes, then break them up.
While the pita are in the oven, make the dressing. Whisk or shake together two tablespoons of extra virgin olive oil, the pomegranate molasses and the juice of the lemon. Peel and crush the garlic clove with the side of your knife and add it to the dressing. Season generously, whisk together then leave to one side. Pick the pomegranate seeds and keep to one side.
Roughly chop the tomatoes, trim and chop the cucumber (if you are using a large cucumber, halve it lengthways and scoop out the middle). Trim and finely slice the spring onions. Pick the parsley leaves and finely chop. Trim and finely slice the radishes. Trim and roughly chop the cos or little gem. Toss everything together with the dressing (discarding the garlic) and spread out onto a platter. Scatter over the toasted pita and the pomegranate seeds and sprinkle over the sumac, then serve.

title: Charred watermelon and pistachio
ingredients:
5 mint sprigs
½ bunch of basil
1 small garlic clove
50g pistachios
1 lemon
Extra virgin olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 green chilli
1kg watermelon
steps:
Pick the mint and basil leaves. Peel the garlic clove. Reserve a few mint and basil leaves, then put the rest of the herbs in a food processor with the garlic, pistachios, juice of the lemon, four tablespoons of extra virgin olive oil and a good pinch of salt and pepper and then pulse until you have a paste that still has a nice bit of coarse, nutty texture. Spoon over a large platter and don’t worry if it feels a little thick, the watermelon will release a lot of liquid.
Halve, deseed and finely slice the chilli, then set aside. Slice the watermelon into 1.5cm-thick slices and cook on the barbecue for around 5 minutes on each side until charred. You can also do this in a hot griddle pan or large dry frying pan. Cut the grilled slices into wedges and place on top of the pistachio pesto. Drizzle with a little extra virgin olive and season. Scatter over the sliced chilli and the reserved mint and basil leaves and serve immediately.

title: Fennel, pear and almond salad
ingredients:
1 teaspoon fennel seeds
40g blanched almonds
½ teaspoon poppy seeds
Olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 fennel bulb
2 crunchy pears (or apples)
2 tablespoons apple cider vinegar
4 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil
80g rocket
steps:
Preheat the oven to 200°C/fan 180°C/gas mark 6. Crush the fennel seeds using a pestle and mortar or spice grinder. Roughly chop the almonds and toss with the crushed fennel seeds, poppy seeds, a little olive oil and season generously. Spread out on a small baking tray and toast in the oven for 8–10 minutes, until the almonds are golden. Remove and set aside to cool.
Trim the fennel bulb of any tough or discoloured bits. Cut the pears of apples into thin wedges, removing core as you go. In a large mixing bowl whisk together the apple cider vinegar and extra virgin olive oil with a good pinch of salt and pepper until combined. Place the fruit wedges on top and then shave in the fennel, using either a mandoline (carefully) or a potato peeler. Add the rocket and toss everything together. Spread out onto a serving plate, scatter over the cooled nuts and seeds and serve straight away.

title: Village-style tomatoes with crisp capers
ingredients:
600g ripe tomatoes (a mixture of sizes and colours if possible)
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
½ red onion
1 tablespoon red wine vinegar
3 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil
2 tablespoon capers
¼ teaspoon dried oregano
steps:
Slice and cut the tomatoes into various chunks, slices and wedges. Place in a colander directly into your sink (or over a mixing bowl) and toss a half-teaspoon of sea salt through the tomatoes. Leave the tomatoes in the colander for 20 minutes, but give them a shake every few minutes, so they release their excess liquid.
Meanwhile, peel and very finely slice the red onion. Place in a large serving bowl and scrunch together with the red wine vinegar and a pinch of salt, then set aside for 10 minutes. Pour one tablespoon of the oil into a small frying or saucepan. Place on a medium heat and fry the drained capers for 3–4 minutes, until they turn a little crisp. Remove from the heat.
When the tomatoes and red onions are ready, mix the remaining two tablespoons of olive oil into the onions. Add the tomatoes to the bowl, season with freshly ground black pepper and sprinkle over the dried oregano. Toss everything together and finish by spooning over the crisp capers and oil from the pan. Serve straight away.

title: Salatet malfouf: a lip-puckering cabbage slaw
ingredients:
½ white cabbage, about 500g
1 onion
8 radishes
1 cucumber
½ bunch of flat-leaf parsley
2 lemons
4 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
½ tablespoon za’atar
steps: Trim the cabbage, remove the core and shred the leaves as finely as you can. Peel, halve and slice the onion just as finely. Trim and finely slice the radishes and cucumber. Finely chop the parsley, stalks and leaves. Squeeze the juice of one and a half lemons into a large mixing bowl and whisk in the extra virgin olive oil till it starts to emulsify, and season generously. Add the finely sliced cabbage and onion, and really scrunch in the dressing. Leave it for 10 minutes, then stir in the sliced radishes, cucumber and chopped parsley. Toss together, and give it a taste. It should be lip-puckeringly lemony, so add more lemon juice as needed and adjust the seasoning. Finish by sprinkling over the za’atar. Unlike most salads, salatet malfouf is even nicer once it has sat for a while, so if you have time, leave it to one side for half an hour before serving.

title: Cooked root vegetable slaw, an addiction
ingredients:
500g beetroot
200g carrots
2 onions
2 garlic cloves
300g tomatoes
100ml sunflower oil
50ml wine vinegar (red or white is fine)
60g granulated sugar
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
½ bunch of dill
steps: Trim, peel and coarsely grate the beetroot and carrots. This is easiest done in a food processor with a grating attachment. However, if you don’t have one you can use a box grater – be prepared for some serious hand stains (consider wearing gloves)! Peel and finely chop the onions and garlic – if you’re using a food processor, you can grate these also. Peel the tomatoes then finely chop them. Place the sunflower oil, wine vinegar and sugar in a large saucepan on a high heat, then add all the grated and chopped vegetables and season generously. Bring to the boil, then reduce to a simmer and cover the pan. Cook for 1½–2 hours, stirring occasionally, until the vegetables are tender. Remove the lid, raise the heat a little and cook for a further 15 minutes, until almost all the liquid has cooked away and the vegetables are soft and look glossy. Remove from the heat and leave to cool. Taste, tweak the seasoning and finely chop the dill. Stir through the dill before serving.

title: Wild mushroom, cherry and buckwheat salad
ingredients:
Sunflower oil
225g buckwheat
450ml hot vegetable stock
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
800g mixed wild mushrooms
4 garlic cloves
1–2 teaspoons pul biber, or dried chilli flakes
1 bunch of spring onions
½ bunch of dill
1 bunch of flat-leaf parsley
2 lemons
80g dried cherries
steps:
Drizzle a little sunflower oil into a large frying pan and toast the buckwheat over a medium heat for 4–5 minutes, until it smells nutty and starts taking on a more golden hue. Spoon the buckwheat into a medium saucepan, pour in the vegetable stock and bring to the boil. Season then cover and reduce the heat a little. Cook for 15 minutes, or until the buckwheat is just tender. Check it a little before and keep an eye on it, otherwise it will turn to mush. When it is ready, remove from the heat. Fork the buckwheat out onto a large plate to cool quickly, so that it doesn’t overcook.
While the buckwheat is cooling, fry the mushrooms. Wipe and trim them. Slice any large ones and leave any nice-looking or exotic ones whole. Peel and finely chop the garlic. Place the large frying pan you toasted the buckwheat in on a medium heat and drizzle in a couple of tablespoons of sunflower oil. Fry the mushrooms for 12–15 minutes, so that they release all their liquid then start to crisp up and turn golden. Add the chopped garlic halfway through, with one teaspoon of pul biber, and generous pinches of salt and pepper (I think it needs at least one teaspoon of flaky sea salt). When the mushrooms are ready, remove the pan from the heat and leave to one side.
Trim and finely slice the spring onions. Pick and roughly chop the dill and parsley leaves. Add them all to a mixing bowl and toss with the cooled buckwheat and fried mushrooms. Squeeze over the juice of both lemons and stir in the dried cherries. Mix everything together, taste and tweak the seasoning, then serve.
source: The Secret to Delicious Vegan Cooking from the Mediterranean and Beyond.epub

title: Griddled red chicory, spelt and pomegranate
ingredients:
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
150g spelt
Extra virgin olive oil
2 shallots
1 pomegranate
½ bunch of flat-leaf parsley
40g walnuts
2 red chicory
3 tablespoons olive oil
1 teaspoon Dijon mustard
2 tablespoons pomegranate molasses
1 tablespoon balsamic vinegar
1 bunch of basil
steps:
Place a large pan of salted water on to boil. Cook the spelt according to the packet instructions and then drain in a sieve. Spoon into a large serving bowl and stir in a little extra virgin olive oil. While the spelt is cooking, get on with the rest of the salad. Peel and finely slice the shallots. Carefully pick the pomegranate seeds from the fruit. Pick and chop the parsley leaves.
Place a large frying pan on a medium heat and toast the walnuts until lightly golden, then transfer to a board and leave to cool. Trim the chicory, slice into quarters, then slice each wedge in half so you end up with thin wedges. Wipe the frying pan clean, drizzle in one tablespoon of olive oil and fry the chicory on a high heat until lightly browned at the edges. You don’t want to sauté them, just cook them quickly to char them a little. Remove from the pan and keep to one side. Pour the remaining olive oil into the pan, add the sliced shallots and turn the heat down to soften. Slowly sauté for 10 minutes, then stir in the mustard, pomegranate molasses and balsamic vinegar. Remove from the heat.
Toss the charred chicory and hot dressing through the spelt along with the pomegranate seeds and chopped parsley. Tear in the basil leaves and season to taste. Chop the toasted walnuts and scatter over the top.
source: The Secret to Delicious Vegan Cooking from the Mediterranean and Beyond.epub

title: Sauerkraut and herb potato salad
ingredients:
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
750g new potatoes
1 garlic clove
1 red onion
2 tablespoons red wine vinegar or cider vinegar
3 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil
1 heaped teaspoon Dijon mustard
2 teaspoons honey (or agave)
100g sauerkraut
½ teaspoon caraway seeds
½ bunch of dill
A few mint or tarragon sprigs
steps:
Bring a large pan of salted water to the boil. Halve and quarter the potatoes, so that they are all a similar size, and place in the pan. Cook for around 15 minutes, until tender. Drain well, and leave to steam dry for 5 minutes.
Meanwhile, peel and finely chop the garlic and red onion. Place in a large mixing bowl with the vinegar and half a teaspoon each of sea salt and freshly ground black pepper. Leave for 5 minutes, then whisk in the extra virgin olive oil, Dijon mustard and honey. Roughly chop the sauerkraut and crush the caraway seeds, and add both to the bowl. Pick the dill and mint or tarragon leaves, finely chop and leave to one side.
When the potatoes are cooked and have steamed dry but are still hot, stir into the dressing. Leave to cool completely, stirring occasionally. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Then when the potatoes have cooled, stir in the chopped fresh herbs and serve.

title: Roast beetroot, lentils and walnuts
ingredients:
600g beetroot, mixed colours if possible
4 red onions
4 garlic cloves
Olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 teaspoon caraway seeds
40g walnuts
150g green or puy lentils
3 tablespoons red wine vinegar
1 teaspoon Dijon mustard
1 teaspoon honey (or maple syrup)
3 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil
½ bunch of flat-leaf parsley
½ bunch of mint
50g wild rocket
steps:
Preheat your oven to 200°C/fan 180°C/gas mark 6. Peel the beetroot and cut into 2–3cm chunks and wedges. Peel and cut the onions into similar sized wedges. Crush the garlic in its skin. Place all the vegetables in a roasting tray and drizzle with olive oil, season well and scatter over the caraway seeds. Toss together and place in the oven for around 50–60 minutes, until caramelised on the edges and the beetroot is cooked through. Place the walnuts in a small tray and toast them in the oven for the last 5 minutes, so they become lightly golden. Remove the two trays from the oven and leave to cool for at least 10 minutes.
Meanwhile, cook the lentils. Give them a rinse in a sieve then place in a pan and add enough cold water to cover by a few centimetres. Bring to the boil, then simmer for 18–20 minutes, until tender but not mushy. Drain the cooked lentils thoroughly. In a large serving bowl, mix the red wine vinegar with the Dijon mustard, honey and extra virgin olive oil, and season. Whisk together then stir in the drained lentils. When the vegetables are ready, toss them through the lentils also. Roughly chop the walnuts. Pick and roughly chop the herb leaves and add them, the walnuts and rocket to the salad just before serving, ideally at room temperature.

title: Green tabbouleh
ingredients:
5 spring onions
2 Greek or Lebanese cucumbers or 1 large English cucumber
2 large bunches of flat-leaf parsley
1 bunch of mint
15 green olives
75g fine bulgur wheat
1 avocado (not too ripe)
2 lemons
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
4 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil
1 romaine or cos lettuce, optional
steps:
Trim and finely chop the spring onions and cucumbers. Trim the parsley stalks, and pick the mint leaves, and chop everything together until very fine. Remove and discard the stones from the olives, and finely chop the flesh. Place everything in a large mixing bowl.
Place the fine bulgur wheat in a bowl and cover with cold water. Leave to soak for 10 minutes, then drain in a sieve and dry on kitchen paper. You don’t want any water in the salad. Peel, destone and finely chop the avocado. Add both to the mixing bowl with the chopped herb mixture and squeeze over the juice from both lemons. Season generously with salt and pepper and drizzle over the extra virgin olive oil. Toss everything together well, then cover and leave in the fridge for at least 30 minutes, or longer, until needed. Serve the tabbouleh as is, or, in lettuce boats. Trim the romaine or cos lettuce, click the leaves apart and wash and dry well. Then fill with the dressed tabbouleh and serve.

title: Roasted garlic muhammara
ingredients:
4 garlic cloves
Extra virgin olive oil
50g walnuts
¾ teaspoon cumin seeds
4 large red peppers
1 red chilli
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
75g white breadcrumbs
4 tablespoons pomegranate molasses
½ lemon
A few pinches of pul biber
A few mint sprigs
steps:
Preheat your oven to 180°C/fan 160°C/gas mark 4. Place the garlic cloves in a small dish (that will also eventually fit the walnuts) and rub them with a little olive oil. Pop in the oven and cook for 20 minutes. Remove the tray, scatter in the walnuts and cumin seeds and return to the oven for 8 minutes, or until the walnuts are golden. Leave to one side to cool. Meanwhile, place the peppers and chilli on an open flame (over your hob or a barbecue) and cook them, turning often so they char evenly. When charred all over, put them in a bowl and cover with cling film. When they are cool enough to handle, peel and discard the skin and seeds. Roughly chop the flesh.
When everything is cool, make the muhammara. Peel the garlic cloves and add to the bowl of a food processor along with the walnuts and cumin seeds. Blitz until roughly chopped. Add the peeled and chopped peppers and chilli and season well. Pulse until everything is just finely chopped together, but you don’t have a sloppy paste. Pulse in the breadcrumbs, two tablespoons of the pomegranate molasses and the juice of the lemon half. When it is all combined, stir in enough extra virgin olive oil to loosen the mixture, and have a taste. Tweak the seasoning, then spoon onto a serving plate. Drizzle with the remaining molasses, a little more oil and sprinkle over the pul biber. Pick and roughly chop the mint leaves and sprinkle over before serving.

title: Classic houmous
ingredients:
500g cooked chickpeas or 500g jarred/tinned chickpeas (drained weight, liquid reserved)
2 garlic cloves
1–2 lemons
100g tahini
Sea salt
Extra virgin olive oil
Paprika, for sprinkling
steps:
When you have cooked your chickpeas according to the method here , leave them in their cooking liquor to cool down. Peeling them here makes all the difference to the end texture.
Whether you’re using cooked dried chickpeas or jarred/tinned ones, drain them in a colander, but keep the liquid. Peel the garlic cloves, then finely grate them into a food processor and squeeze in the juice of 1 lemon. Add the tahini and a good splash of the chickpea water and blitz till you have a pale, loose paste. Add the drained chickpeas and a generous pinch of salt and blitz until creamy. Taste and add more salt and lemon juice. If it feels a little thick and grainy, add a small splash of chickpea water (not too much or you could end up with a sloppy mess; you can always add a little more). When the houmous has the flavour and texture you like, spoon it on to a serving plate, then drizzle with extra virgin olive oil and sprinkle with paprika.

title: Tsakistes: lemon and coriander marinated olives
ingredients:
500g small green olives (either fresh or in brine)
50ml extra virgin olive oil
2 lemons
3 garlic cloves
2 teaspoons coriander seeds
Sea salt
steps:
If you are using the fresh young green olives, prepare them as instructed in the introduction. Alternatively just drain the preserved ones and place them in a bowl. Stir in the extra virgin olive oil and squeeze in the juice of half of one of the lemons. Cut the remaining lemon half into two, then slice into 1cm half-moon slices. Crush the garlic with the flat of your knife, remove the skin and stir the cloves into the olives with the lemon slices. Crush the coriander seeds – doesn’t need to be too fine, crushed and halved is fine – and add to the bowl also. Stir all together, taste and season with salt to taste and add more lemon juice if needed. You can serve immediately, or ideally leave for a few days so the olives really take on all the flavours. If that is the case, store the olives covered in the fridge, then leave at room temperature for a few hours before serving.
I like to serve mine with finely chopped fresh coriander stirred through, and sprinkled with a pinch of pul biber or chilli flakes.

title: Baka Mara’s meljanac: crushed beans with paprika and garlic
ingredients:
200g dried cannellini beans or 2 × 400g jars/tins of beans
1 carrot
1 onion
3 bay leaves
A few black peppercorns
Sea salt
8 tablespoons sunflower oil
1 tablespoon plain flour
1 heaped teaspoon sweet paprika
2 garlic cloves
steps:
Soak the dried beans overnight in plenty of cold water.
The next day, drain the beans and add them to a medium-sized saucepan and cover with fresh water. Peel and roughly chop the carrot and half the onion and add to the pan with the bay leaves and peppercorns. Bring to the boil on a high heat, then reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer gently for 1–1½ hours, or until the beans are tender. When the beans are cooked, drain them in a colander and take out the vegetables, bay leaves and peppercorns. If you’re using tinned or jarred beans, drain them, then start from here. Return the beans to the saucepan and use a potato masher to crush them into a paste. This should be quite smooth, but not smushed to a fine purée. Season with salt to taste.
Peel and finely chop the remaining onion half. Add four tablespoons of the oil to a medium frying pan; ideally, you want at least 5mm covering the base of your pan. Place the pan over a medium-low heat and gently fry the chopped onion for around 10 minutes so that it softens and turns only very lightly golden. Quickly stir in the plain flour and paprika until you have a paste then remove from the heat, as burning the onions and paprika will make it bitter. Pour the roux over the mashed beans and mix in well. Taste and adjust the seasoning as needed, then spoon the beans into a serving dish. Wipe out the frying pan with kitchen paper, then return to the hob and add four more tablespoons of oil. Peel and finely slice the garlic cloves and add to the pan. Fry them gently on a low heat, then when they’re just turning golden pour the garlic and the infused oil over the crushed beans. Serve straight away – I like this on toast, or just with a pile of toasted flatbread or pita for scooping it up.

title: Tashi, teradot, toum: a tale of three garlic sauces
ingredients:
150g tahini
1–2 garlic cloves
1 lemon
2 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground white pepper
A few flat-leaf parsley sprigs, optional
2 garlic cloves (or 3 roasted cloves)
125g walnuts
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
3 tablespoons tahini
2 lemons
1 large bunch of flat-leaf parsley
Extra virgin olive oil
1 head of garlic
1 teaspoon sea salt
1 lemon
400ml vegetable or sunflower oil (or any flavourless oil)
3 ice cubes (or 3 tablespoons iced water)
steps:
Spoon the tahini into a mixing bowl. Peel and finely grate in the garlic clove (adding another if you like your sauces quite punchy). Whisk together, then slowly pour in 160ml of just-boiled water, whisking it in the whole time until smooth. You will end up with a pale, thick dip. Squeeze in the juice of the lemon, and add a tablespoon of the extra virgin olive oil. Mix in and season to taste. Place the tashi in the fridge for at least 1 hour, to thicken slightly. Serve drizzled with the remaining extra virgin olive oil, and a sprinkle of chopped parsley, if you like.
Peel and finely chop the garlic, then add to the bowl of a food processor with the walnuts, plus a quarter-teaspoon each of sea salt and freshly ground black pepper. Blitz until very finely ground. Add the tahini to the bowl and pulse in until you have a paste. Scoop the mixture into a bowl and stir in the juice of both the lemons and four tablespoons of boiling water. Mix together well, until you have a creamy sauce. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Pick and very finely chop the flat-leaf parsley leaves and stir into the sauce. Garnish with a drizzle of extra virgin olive oil and a few sprigs of parsley, if you have some left.
Peel all the garlic cloves. If you’re using a mini food processor, place all the garlic in the bowl and blitz along with the sea salt until very finely chopped. Then squeeze in the lemon juice (discarding the pips) and blitz in until you have a smooth paste.
If you are using a large pestle and mortar, halve the ingredients or make this in two batches. Roughly chop the garlic first then place in the mortar with the salt and bash until creamy and smooth. Pound in the lemon juice until you have a paste.
Whichever method you are using, the next step is key. Working slowly, either with the food processor motor running, or just making sure you take your time, blitz or pound the vegetable oil into the garlic paste. If using the food processor, drizzle the oil into the opening on the top in a very slow and steady stream. After you have added about 150ml, add an ice cube to the bowl and blitz in. Repeat until you have used all the oil and ice cubes – this should take 10 minutes or so.
If making it by hand, follow the same instructions, working in thirds, but instead of an ice cube, use a tablespoon of iced water. The toum is ready when it is white, fluffy, light in texture and emulsified.

title: Apple, fennel and dill sauerkraut
ingredients:
1 teaspoon fennel seeds
1 white cabbage, about 800g
1½ tablespoons fine sea salt
1 fennel bulb
1 Granny Smith apple
1 bunch of dill
steps:
Sterilise your jar . Toast the fennel seeds in a small dry pan over a low heat for a couple of minutes, then leave to one side to cool. Remove the outer leaves from the cabbage, keeping one leaf aside for later, and cut the rest into quarters. Turn onto a cut edge, and finely slice using a sharp knife or mandolin. Place in a large mixing bowl with the sea salt, massage it all in and leave to one side to wilt slightly.
While the cabbage is being salted, trim the fennel bulb, slice in half and finely slice also. Halve, remove the core from the apple and finely slice also. Roughly chop the dill. Add it all to the bowl with the cabbage, plus the toasted fennel seeds, and mix together – you should notice liquid in the bottom of the bowl. Mix and massage it all together for 5 minutes, to ensure more juices are released.
Pack the mixture into your jar, layering it up and pressing down with your fist as you go so there are no pockets of air. By this point the cabbage should have released enough of its own liquid to be fully submerged in its own juices. When you are finished, place the reserved leaf over the top, and something heavy to weight down the mixture, like a small ramekin. Close the jar tightly and leave to ferment out of direct sunlight at room temperature for 10–14 days, opening to release the gases every other day. Taste the cabbage after 10 days and leave to ferment for longer if needed. Once you are happy with the taste, transfer the jar to the fridge to slow down the fermentation process. It will keep in the cold for up to 6 months.

title: Ajvar
ingredients:
2 aubergines
4 red peppers
3 garlic cloves
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
5 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil, plus extra to serve
½ tablespoon red or white wine vinegar
½ teaspoon dried chilli flakes, optional, plus extra to serve
steps:
You can cook the vegetables under the grill or, if you’d rather, in the oven. I prefer the flavour under the grill, but the oven is less time consuming. For the grill, preheat it to medium-high heat, and if cooking in the oven preheat it to its highest setting.
Pierce the aubergines all over with a sharp knife. Place under the grill with the red peppers and grill for around 30–40 minutes, turning several times, until blackened all over. If roasting in the oven, place the veg directly on the oven bars and roast for 20–30 minutes, until blackened. When they are all ready, place the red peppers in a bowl and cover with cling film. Leave for 10 minutes and then peel off the pepper skins. Roughly chop the flesh, discarding the stalk and seeds. Leave the aubergine to cool slightly. When it is cool enough to handle, remove the top, scoop out the flesh and discard the skin. Peel and chop the garlic. Blitz all the vegetables in a food processor and until finely chopped and creamy looking. Add half a teaspoon each of salt and pepper, the extra virgin olive oil, vinegar and chilli (if using) and blitz again. Spoon the mixture into a pan and gently cook gently over a low heat for 30–40 minutes, to thicken up. Leave to cool completely before serving. Serve with a drizzle of extra virgin olive oil and the dried chilli on top.

title: Marinated wild mushrooms
ingredients:
1kg wild, or mixed, mushrooms
4 garlic cloves
175ml olive oil
100ml red wine vinegar
1 tablespoon coriander seeds
4 oregano sprigs or ½ teaspoon dried oregano
¼ teaspoon chilli flakes or pul biber
2 bay leaves
1 teaspoon peppercorns
1 teaspoon sea salt
steps: Start by sterilising one large or two medium jars, as directed here ; if you plan on eating them straight away or over a few days, you can just keep this in an airtight container in the fridge. Next prepare the mushrooms. Wipe them clean, trim the ends and halve or quarter any larger ones. If you are using very large mushrooms, then slice them into 2cm-thick slices. Crush the garlic, in its skin, with the side of your knife, then add it to a large saucepan with the olive oil. Place on a medium-low heat and fry the whole cloves for 2–3 minutes, until you can start to smell them. Add all the remaining ingredients apart from the prepared mushrooms, and turn the heat up. Bring to the boil, then add the mushrooms. Cook for 6 minutes, then remove from the heat. Ladle straight into the sterilised jars – try to evenly distribute the aromatics if possible – then seal the jars while still hot. Leave to cool, and store in a dark cupboard. Once opened, transfer the jar to the fridge.

title: Moungra: fermented cauliflower in mustard seeds
ingredients:
1 × 7g sachet of fast-action dried yeast
100g strong white bread flour
1½ tablespoons fine sea salt
or 300g levain
1kg cauliflower
Ice
2 tablespoons yellow mustard seeds
steps:
You will need a very large preserving jar for this – traditionally it would be made in a large crock or something similar. Mix the yeast into 200ml warm water and leave to one side. Mix the flour with a half-tablespoon of the salt in a large mixing bowl and then whisk in the yeast water until completely smooth. Cover the bowl with cling film and leave in a cool dark place for 3–4 days to ferment. (If using levain you can skip this step).
When ready to make the moungra, prepare the cauliflower. Remove any leaves and cut into florets, discarding the main large piece of stem – you should have around 700g of cauliflower at this stage. Place the florets in a bowl of iced water for 15 minutes. Bring a large pan of salted water to the boil. Using a slotted spoon, place the cauliflower florets into the boiling water for 2 minutes, then spoon them out and place back into the iced water. Once they are all cooked and cool, drain and leave to dry on a tea towel. Meanwhile, place 1 litre of water to boil. Slowly whisk the boiling water into the levain or yeast-flour mixture, until smooth and milky. Crush the mustard seeds in a pestle and mortar. You don’t have to finely grind them, just crush.
To assemble the moungra, sterilise your large jar or crock (see here ). Sprinkle some of the mustard seeds into the base, then add a layer of the blanched and dried cauliflower florets, then a sprinkling of sea salt. Repeat until the pot or jar is full, or you have used up all the ingredients. Carefully ladle in the yeast or sourdough water (using a funnel if you have one) until all the cauliflower is covered. Place the lid on and leave the pot in a cool dark spot for 8–10 days, turning the jar every day, and giving it a little shake. If you are using a crock, cover with a greaseproof lid, and put your (clean) hand in every day and turn the florets individually.
Taste the cauliflower; it should taste slightly sour and salty. Serve in a small bowl, drizzled with a little extra virgin olive oil on top. Store any extra moungra in the fridge to slow down the fermentation process. It will keep there for a good few months.

title: Spiced snacking nuts and seeds
ingredients:
¼ teaspoon black peppercorns
1 teaspoon nigella seeds
1 teaspoon aniseed or fennel seeds
1 teaspoon cumin seeds
¼ teaspoon sweet paprika
60g caster sugar
1–2 teaspoons sea salt (1 teaspoon if fine, 2 teaspoons if flaky)
1 tablespoon olive oil
200g shelled nuts, a mixture
50g mixed seeds
steps:
Preheat your oven to 200°C/fan 180°C/gas mark 6. Line a baking tray with greaseproof paper. Place the black peppercorns, nigella seeds, aniseed and cumin seeds in a mortar and crush with a pestle until ground but still with a little texture – do not let the mixture get too fine. Place the mixture in a small saucepan with the paprika, sugar, sea salt, olive oil and 50ml of water. Bring to the boil on a medium heat, then add all the nuts and seeds, give it a good stir and cook for a further 2–3 minutes until glossy.
Spoon the coated nuts onto the baking tray, making sure they are in one layer, then pop into the oven for 8–10 minutes, stirring halfway through. Leave to cool completely before eating, or store in an airtight container.

title: Spiced onion oil
ingredients:
2 bunches of spring onions
1 leek
400ml vegetable oil
2 tablespoons baharat for how to make your own)
1 heaped tablespoon caster sugar
1 teaspoon sea salt
steps: Trim the spring onions then slice into 2cm lengths. Trim and finely slice the green part of the leek. Slice the white section into 1cm rings, then place all the leek in a colander and rinse thoroughly under cold running water to get rid of any dirt, then shake off and leave to dry on a clean tea towel. Place all the sliced alliums in a saucepan with the vegetable oil and put on a medium-low heat. You don’t want to cook the onions and leeks too fast, rather infuse the oil and let them gently turn a very light golden colour. This should take around 15–20 minutes. When they are ready, stir in the baharat, caster sugar and salt and reduce the heat to low. Cook for a further 3 minutes. Remove the pan from the heat and leave to cool. Store in an airtight container or jar in the fridge and spoon out as and when needed.

title: Ladolemono: lemon, oregano and olive oil dressing
ingredients:
3 lemons
1 garlic clove
100ml extra virgin olive oil
½ teaspoon dried oregano
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
steps: Squeeze the lemons into a mixing bowl and discard the pips. You ideally want three or four tablespoons of juice. Peel the garlic clove, and crush it with the flat side of your knife. Add it to the bowl with the extra virgin olive oil, the dried oregano and a generous pinch each of sea salt and freshly ground black pepper. Whisk it all together and have a taste – if you are using it for salad leaves then season it generously. Either using straight away or transfer to a jam jar, keeping in the garlic clove, seal and store in the fridge until needed.

title: Dukkah
ingredients:
150g nuts, a mix of types
1 teaspoon fennel seeds
2 tablespoons sesame seeds
2 tablespoons coriander seeds
1 tablespoon cumin seeds
1 teaspoon nigella seeds
¼ teaspoon cayenne pepper, optional
2 teaspoons flaky sea salt or 1 teaspoon fine sea salt
1 teaspoon coarsely ground black pepper
steps: Place the nuts in a dry frying pan and toast over a medium heat for around 3–4 minutes, until golden and toasted all over. Place in the bowl of a food processor and leave to cool as you toast the spices. Place the fennel, sesame, coriander, cumin and nigella seeds in the pan and toast for just a couple of minutes until you can really smell them. Remove from the heat and leave in the pan for a minute while you pulse the nuts. Pulse a few times to roughly chop, then add the toasted seeds, along with the remaining ingredients and pulse until roughly chopped and well combined. Do not let this become too fine, or it will turn into a paste. Transfer to an airtight container.

title: Baharat, za’atar and Lebanese seven-spice
ingredients:
15 green cardamom pods
1½ teaspoons black peppercorns
1 tablespoon cumin seeds
2 teaspoons coriander seeds
1 teaspoon ground cinnamon
¼ teaspoon ground cloves
1 tablespoon sweet paprika
½ nutmeg
2 tablespoons sesame seeds
2 tablespoons dried wild thyme or oregano
2 tablespoons sumac
1 teaspoon flaked sea salt
1 tablespoon peppercorns
2 teaspoons cumin seeds
2 tablespoons coriander seeds
1 tablespoon ground allspice
1 tablespoon ground cinnamon
½ teaspoon ground cloves
½ nutmeg
steps:
Remove the seeds from the cardamom pods, and discard the husks. Place the seeds in a small dry pan with the peppercorns, cumin seeds and coriander seeds and toast over a low heat for a couple of minutes until fragrant. Remove from the pan and leave to cool. When they are ready, grind using a pestle and mortar until fine, then mix in the ground cinnamon, ground cloves and sweet paprika. Finely grate in the nutmeg and mix well. Store in an airtight container and use as needed.
Toast the sesame seeds in a large dry frying pan over a medium heat until very lightly golden, then leave to cool. When they’re ready, mix in the dried herbs, sumac and salt and store in an airtight container.
Toast the peppercorns, cumin seeds and coriander seeds in a small dry frying pan over a low heat for a couple of minutes until fragrant. After a couple of minutes, remove from the heat, leave to cool then finely grind them. Stir in the remaining ground spices and finely grate in the nutmeg. Mix everything together and store in an airtight container until needed.

title: Bećar paprikaš: slow-cooked peppers
ingredients:
4 onions
4 garlic cloves
10 peppers, a mixture of red, yellow and orange ones
5 ripe tomatoes
100ml sunflower oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
A few flat-leaf parsley sprigs, optional
steps:
Peel and finely slice the onions and garlic. Halve the peppers, remove and discard the core and seeds, and cut into even sized pieces, around 2–3cm. Score a cross in the top of the tomatoes, place in a heatproof bowl (or pan) and cover with boiling water. Leave for a minute or two, until the skin starts to come away from the flesh, and drain. Peel the tomatoes and then roughly slice or chop the flesh.
Place a wide flameproof casserole on a medium heat, drizzle in the sunflower oil and add all the ingredients. Season generously, with a teaspoon each of salt and pepper, and start to fry. After 10 minutes, reduce the heat to low and fry for around 1½–2 hours. Stir occasionally, until you have a thick, rich and meltingly soft stew. Taste and tweak the seasoning as necessary, then serve, scattered with chopped parsley, if you like.

title: Braised fennel with saffron
ingredients:
A pinch of saffron threads
2 fennel bulbs
Olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 tablespoon honey (or agave, maple syrup or sugar)
½ bunch of flat-leaf parsley
2 tablespoons harissa paste
steps:
Place the saffron threads in 350ml of just-boiled water and set aside to infuse.
Pick any fennel fronds (the little frilly green herb in the middle of the bulb) from the fennel bulbs and keep to one side. Trim the ends and base of the fennel bulbs and cut them into quarters. Lay the wedges out in one layer in a large frying pan and drizzle with a little olive oil, season generously, turn to coat, and place the pan on a medium heat. Fry the fennel for around 10 –12 minutes, turning halfway through, until lightly browned all over. Drizzle with the honey and cook for a further 3–4 minutes so the wedges become slightly caramelised. Pour the saffron water into the pan, turn up the heat to bring to the boil, then cover the pan and reduce the heat to low-medium and simmer gently for 15–20 minutes, until the fennel is tender.
Meanwhile, pick and roughly chop the flat-leaf parsley and keep to one side. When the fennel is cooked through, remove the lid and increase the heat to cook away most of the liquid, leaving 5mm at the bottom. Turn the heat off and leave the fennel in the pan to cool slightly. Spoon the harissa onto a serving plate and lay the fennel wedges on top, spoon over a little of the pan juices and sprinkle with the flat-leaf parsley leaves and reserved fennel fronds.

title: Sweet and sour leeks
ingredients:
3 leeks
3 garlic cloves
4 tablespoons olive oil
1 tablespoon caster sugar
2 thyme or oregano sprigs, ideally the wild varieties
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 lemon
steps: Trim the leeks, finely slice the green end and slice the white end into 2cm rounds. Place it all in a colander and rinse thoroughly under cold running water to get rid of any dirt. Peel and finely slice the garlic. Place a large saucepan on a medium-low heat and add the olive oil and sliced garlic. Fry for a minute, then add the sugar and fry for a further 1–2 minutes or until the garlic is lightly golden. Add the washed leeks, pick in the thyme or oregano leaves, and season with a good few pinches of salt and pepper. Fry for about 5 minutes, then add 75ml water, cover with a lid and reduce the heat to low. Cook for 30 minutes or so, stirring from time to time, until softened and sticky. After half an hour, remove the lid, turn the heat up a little and cook for 5 more minutes to get rid of any excess liquid. Squeeze and stir in the juice of the lemon. Taste and tweak the seasoning, then serve.

title: Baklazhannaia ikra: poor man’s caviar
ingredients:
3 aubergines, about 1kg
5 tablespoons sunflower oil
2 red peppers
2 carrots
4 onions
6 garlic cloves
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
4 ripe tomatoes
2 tablespoons pepper or sun-dried tomato paste
steps:
Preheat the oven to 190°C/fan 170°C/gas mark 5. Pierce the aubergines all over with a fork. Rub with a little sunflower oil and place them in a roasting tray. Pop in the oven for 1 hour, turning them halfway through. When they are soft and cooked through, remove them from the oven and leave to one side to cool slightly.
Meanwhile, halve the peppers, remove the stalk and seeds and finely chop the flesh. Peel and coarsely grate the carrots. Peel and finely slice the onions and garlic cloves. Place a large saucepan on a medium-low heat and add the sunflower oil. Add all of the chopped, grated and sliced vegetables, season well and sauté for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until soft and sticky. If it starts to look a bit dry or starts catching, turn the heat right down and cover the pan, stirring occasionally. Finely chop the tomatoes, then stir them into the pan with the pepper or sun-dried tomato paste and continue to cook the vegetables for a further 10 minutes.
When the aubergines are cool enough to handle, cut in half and use a fork to scoop out the filling, shredding it as you go. Shred it directly into a colander in your sink, and press the roasted flesh lightly to get rid of any liquid. Spoon the drained, roasted aubergines into the pan with all the vegetables, and stir everything together. Reduce the heat to low, then cover the pan and cook for 1 hour, stirring often so that it doesn’t catch on the bottom. You want the end result to be a rich, thick paste with no liquid in the pan. If it is still a little wet, stir uncovered with the heat turned up a little until it is ready. Taste and adjust the seasoning.

title: Skordoxithia koukia: vinegar-braised broad beans
ingredients:
2.5kg broad beans (podded weight about 500g – frozen is fine)
2 garlic cloves
3 tablespoons olive oil
2 tablespoons plain flour
1 heaped tablespoon tomato purée
3 tablespoons white or red wine vinegar
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
½ bunch of dill or flat-leaf parsley
steps: Pod the broad beans. If they are young, don’t worry about double-podding them. However if they are on the larger side, peel off the outer grey skins so you just have the vibrant green beans. Peel and finely chop the garlic. Place a large saucepan on a medium-low heat and add the olive oil and chopped garlic. Fry for a minute or two, until very lightly golden then stir in the plain flour and tomato purée. Fry for a couple of minutes, stirring all the while to make a paste, then stir in the vinegar. Add the broad beans, give them a stir, then add just enough water to cover. Season with sea salt and freshly ground black pepper and bring to the boil. Once boiling, reduce the heat and simmer uncovered for 15–20 minutes, until the beans are cooked and the water has evaporated and thickened to create a perfect dressing. Taste, adjust the seasoning, and leave to cool a little. Finely chop the dill or flat-leaf parsley and stir through. This can be served warm or at room temperature.
