title: Yiahni: braised peas and other vegetables
ingredients:
600g potatoes, Cyprus ideally
80–100ml olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
2 onions
2 garlic cloves
4 carrots
5 ripe tomatoes or 1 x 400g tin of plum tomatoes
1 heaped tablespoon tomato purée
600g baby peas
1 bay leaf
500ml vegetable stock
A few flat-leaf parsley sprigs
steps:
Peel the potatoes and cut into large chunks, around 5cm. Pour enough olive oil into a large saucepan or casserole to fill it by 1cm, around 80ml. Place on a medium heat, and fry the potatoes, seasoning as you go, until browned on all sides. Remove from the pan and keep to one side.
Meanwhile, peel and finely slice the onions and garlic. Peel and roughly chop the carrots. If using fresh tomatoes, peel them (see here ), then roughly chop and keep to one side. After the potatoes are browned, add the onions, garlic and carrots to the same pan, reduce the heat a little and sauté for 10 minutes to soften slightly. Stir in the tomato purée, then after a minute add the chopped or tinned tomatoes, the peas, bay leaf and the vegetable stock. Bring to the boil and let it bubble for 5 minutes, then reduce the heat to low, cover with a lid and simmer for 45 minutes. Check the vegetables: everything should be tender and the liquid thickened. If it still looks a little watery, remove the lid, turn the heat up a little and cook uncovered for 5–10 minutes to reduce down. Remove from the heat and leave for at least 10 minutes before serving. Finely chop the parsley and stir through. Check the seasoning, adding more if need be, and then serve.

title: Loubye b’zeit: slow-cooked runner beans with olives
ingredients:
2 onions
4 garlic cloves
600g runner beans
8 ripe tomatoes
5 tablespoons olive oil
1 tablespoon tomato purée
½ teaspoon ground cinnamon
¼ teaspoon ground allspice
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
70g pitted black olives
½ tablespoon red wine vinegar
steps:
Peel and finely chop the onions and garlic. Top and tail the runner beans, removing the stringy fibre that runs down the side, then chop into 4cm lengths. Chop the tomatoes into 2cm pieces (ideally peeling them first, see here , but if you don’t it’s not the end of the world).
Pour the olive oil into a large flameproof casserole or big saucepan and place over a medium-low heat. Add the chopped onions and garlic and sauté for 15 minutes, until starting to soften. Stir in the chopped beans, fry for 5 minutes, then add the tomato purée, ground cinnamon and ground allspice. Fry for 1 minute before adding the chopped tomatoes and 300ml of boiling water. Bring to the boil, season generously with salt and pepper and tear in the olives. Once bubbling, reduce the heat to low and cover the pan. Simmer for 30 minutes, until the runner beans are tender. Remove the lid, and turn the heat up to reduce the sauce further if it is still a little watery. Stir in the vinegar, taste and adjust the seasoning. Finish with a good drizzle of extra virgin olive oil and serve once it has cooled a little.

title: Briam
ingredients:
600g Cyprus or other waxy potatoes (you can use small waxy potatoes if that’s all you can find)
2 courgettes
4 ripe tomatoes
2 aubergines
2 red onions
2 red peppers
½ bunch of flat-leaf parsley
2 heaped tablespoons tomato purée
1 heaped teaspoon dried oregano
½ teaspoon pul biber, optional
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
6 tablespoons olive oil
steps:
Preheat the oven to 210°C/fan 190°C/gas mark 6½. If the potatoes are large, you can scrub or peel them if you like – I like to leave the skin on. Cut them into 2cm-thick slices. Slice the courgettes, tomatoes and aubergines into 1cm-thick rounds, discarding the ends, then peel and finely slice the onions. Halve and deseed the peppers and slice into 1cm strips. Pick and chop the parsley leaves and keep to one side, then finely slice the stalks and keep them separate from the leaves. Dissolve the tomato purée in 200ml of just-boiled water.
Place all the sliced vegetables in a large roasting tray. Scatter over the chopped parsley stalks, the dried oregano and the pul biber if using, and season generously with about a teaspoon each of salt and pepper. Drizzle over the olive oil, and massage everything together to evenly distribute the flavours. Spread everything into an even layer and pour over the tomato water. Place in the oven and cook for 1½ hours, checking every 30 minutes to give it all a mix around with a large spoon. The briam is ready when the vegetables are soft but slightly crisp around the edges. If it isn’t quite ready, give it another 15–20 minutes. When it’s cooked, leave to cool for at least 20 minutes, before finishing with the remaining chopped parsley leaves.

title: Spiced roasted okra, molasses and herbs
ingredients:
500g okra
½ teaspoon pul biber or dried chilli flakes
¼ teaspoon sweet paprika
1 tablespoon red wine vinegar
3 tablespoons olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
4 spring onions
½ bunch of coriander
½ bunch of mint
1 tbsp pomegranate molasses
2 tablespoons pomegranate seeds
steps:
Preheat your oven to 240°C/fan 220°C/gas mark 9. Trim the okra by removing the stalk and snipping off the very tip. Place the spears in a large roasting tray, sprinkle over the pul biber and paprika and drizzle with the red wine vinegar and the olive oil. Season generously and toss everything together well, then spread the okra out evenly. Place the tray in the oven and roast for 20–25 minutes, giving it a shake a couple of times.
While the okra is roasting, trim and finely slice the spring onions. Pick and roughly chop the coriander and mint leaves. When the okra is ready and starting to look crisp, drizzle with the pomegranate molasses as soon as it comes out of the oven. Toss through the sliced spring onion, and serve with the herbs and pomegranate seeds piled on top.

title: Grilled squash with herbs and dukkah
ingredients:
800g butternut squash
3 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
½ bunch of flat-leaf parsley
½ bunch of mint
1 lemon
2 tablespoons dukkah (for how to make your own)
steps:
Place a grill pan on a high heat. Peel and slice the squash into 1cm slices, discarding any seeds. Place in a large bowl and drizzle with two tablespoons of extra virgin olive oil and season generously with salt and pepper. Massage the seasoning into the squash, then grill the slices for 3–4 minutes on each side, until charred in parts and just cooked through. You will have to do this in batches. When the squash is ready, transfer to a platter.
While it is cooking, pick the herb leaves into a mixing bowl and finely grate over the lemon zest. Squeeze over the lemon juice, stir in the remaining olive oil, season a little and toss together. When all the squash is cooked, toss through the herb mixture and sprinkle with the dukkah.

title: Maroulla’s spiced courgettes
ingredients:
3 garlic cloves
1 onion
500g courgettes
3 tablespoons olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
½ teaspoon Lebanese seven-spice (for how to make your own)
¼ teaspoon pul biber or dried chilli flakes
steps: Peel and finely slice the garlic cloves and onion. Trim the courgettes then cut into 2–3cm thick slices or chunks. My favourite way is to cut them in small wedges: so slice off the top straight, then slice the next piece of courgette at 45-degree angle, next slice straight, next at an angle. Pour the olive oil into a wide frying or saucepan on a medium-low heat and add the garlic. Place on a medium-low heat and fry for a few minutes, until the garlic is lightly golden. Add the sliced onion and courgettes to the pan and season generously with salt and pepper. Turn the heat up to medium and fry for a couple of minutes, then cover the pan with a lid. Cook for 10 minutes, covered, stirring halfway through. Then remove the lid, stir in the spices, reduce the heat lightly and fry for a further 10–15 minutes so that any liquid cooks away, and the vegetables are soft, sticky and golden around the edges. The courgettes should almost be falling apart and very soft. Taste and adjust the seasoning, then serve.

title: Arnabeet: deep-fried cauliflower with tarator
ingredients:
1 large head of cauliflower (around 1kg with leaves)
1 litre vegetable oil
¼ teaspoon sweet smoked paprika
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 teaspoon sumac
½ bunch of flat-leaf parsley
1 lemon
1 garlic clove
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
3 tablespoons tahini
1 lemon
steps:
Cut the cauliflower into equal-sized florets and wash well with cold water. Spread out on a tea towel and leave to dry completely. Meanwhile, make the tarator dressing. Peel and roughly chop the garlic clove and place in a pestle and mortar. Pound till creamy with a good pinch of salt and pepper then muddle in the tahini and the juice of the lemon. Add two tablespoons of cold water and mix together, adding more if it is too thick – you’re looking for something about the consistency of double cream or slightly thicker. Taste and adjust the seasoning, then set aside until ready to serve.
When you are ready to fry the cauliflower, pour the oil into a large saucepan and place on a medium heat. Line a large plate with kitchen paper. Place the cauliflower pieces in a large bowl, sprinkle over the paprika and season generously with a few good pinches of salt and pepper. Toss the cauliflower until all the florets are coated. Place a small piece of cauliflower into the oil and when it starts to sizzle and turn golden brown, the oil is ready. If you have a thermometer, the oil should be about 170°C, then when you add the cauliflower it will drop to about 160°C. Fry the seasoned cauliflower florets in batches, so as to not overcrowd the pan, for 4–5 minutes, until crisp and golden all over. Transfer them to the paper-lined plate. When all the florets are cooked, pile them up on a platter or serving plate, sprinkle with sumac and drizzle over the tarator sauce. Roughly chop the parsley and scatter it over. Cut the lemon into wedges, and serve on the side, for squeezing over.

title: Eleni’s artichoke tava
ingredients:
2 lemons
6–8 violet or small globe artichokes
4 carrots
3 large onions
5 ripe tomatoes
100ml sunflower or olive oil
2 tablespoons tomato purée
1 tablespoon ground cumin
1 teaspoon ground cinnamon
200g medium or long grain rice
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
A few flat-leaf parsley sprigs
steps:
Halve one of the lemons and squeeze all of the juice into a large bowl of water – you’ll need this to prepare the artichokes. Using a serrated knife, trim off the top of the artichokes and a good chunk of the stem. Peel or cut away the tough outer leaves, leaving the tender inner leaves. Trim down the stem to remove the tough skin. Then halve the artichokes and use a teaspoon to scoop out the choke (the fuzzy bit in the middle). Cut the artichokes into 2cm-thick slices, and rub them with the cut lemon halves to stop them browning, then place them in the water.
Peel the carrots and slice into 2cm-thick rounds. Peel and slice the onions into 2cm-thick wedges. Score the tops of the tomatoes with a cross and submerge into a bowl of just-boiled water. Leave to one side for 5 minutes, then drain and peel off the skin. Roughly chop the flesh.
Preheat your oven to 190°C/fan 170°C/gas mark 5. Place a wide flameproof casserole dish (that has a lid) on a medium heat and pour in the oil. Fry the drained sliced artichokes for 8–10 minutes, until lightly golden, then add the onions and carrots and turn the heat down a little. Fry for 5 minutes then stir in the tomato purée and chopped tomatoes. Fry for a couple of minutes, then stir in the cumin and cinnamon, and then stir in the rice. Season generously and keep stirring until all the rice is coated with the oil and flavourings and well mixed in with the vegetables. Meanwhile, boil a kettle then pour in 700ml of boiling water, so that the rice is just covered, and cover the dish. Place in the oven and cook for 25 minutes, so that everything is perfectly cooked. Remove the lid, turn the oven temperature up to 220°C/fan 200°C/gas mark 7 and cook for a further 10 minutes until gold and crisp on top. Leave to rest for 5 minutes. Roughly chop the parsley, and serve scattered over the tava, with the remaining lemon cut in wedges on the side.

title: Crushed coriander and olive potatoes
ingredients:
750g new potatoes
2 teaspoons coriander seeds
Olive oil
½ lemon
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
60g pitted black olives, such as kalamata
½ bunch of coriander, optional
steps: Preheat the oven to 220°C/fan 200°C/gas mark 7. Bring a large pan of salted water to the boil. Place the potatoes in the pan and boil for 15 minutes, or until almost cooked through. Drain and leave them to steam dry in the hot pan. Transfer to a roasting tray and carefully crush the potatoes, either with the heel of your hand or with the back of spoon or a fish slice. Crush the coriander seeds using a pestle and mortar (these don’t have to be too fine) and sprinkle over the potatoes with a few tablespoons of olive oil, the juice of the lemon and a good amount of seasoning. Tear in the olives, toss to combine, then roast for 20–25 minutes, until golden and crisp. When the potatoes are ready, roughly chop the coriander leaves, if you like, then scatter and serve.

title: Batata harra: chilli-dressed potatoes
ingredients:
800g large waxy potatoes, Cyprus or red-skinned ideally
Olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 onion
3 garlic cloves
1 bunch of coriander
1 teaspoon pul biber or dried chilli flakes
¼ teaspoon sweet smoked paprika
¼ teaspoon turmeric
½ lemon
steps:
Preheat your oven to 210°C/fan 190°C/gas mark 6½. Traditionally, the potatoes would be peeled, but I like leaving the skin on, so it’s up to you. Cut the potatoes in 3cm cubes and place in a roasting tray big enough to hold them in one layer, then drizzle with a couple of tablespoons of olive oil. Season, toss together well, and place in the oven for 50 minutes, or until golden all over and cooked through.
While the potatoes are cooking, make the dressing. Peel and finely chop the onion and garlic. Pick the coriander leaves, finely chop the stalks and roughly chop the leaves. Place a small frying pan on a medium-low heat and drizzle in three tablespoons of olive oil. Add the chopped onion and garlic and sauté for 15 minutes until starting to soften (if it starts to catch, add a splash of water). Stir in the pul biber, sweet smoked paprika, turmeric, the finely chopped coriander stalks and half the coriander leaves, and fry for a further minute then remove from the heat. When the potatoes are ready, stir through the cooked garlic mixture and the remaining chopped coriander. Squeeze over the juice from the lemon and serve immediately.

title: Taro two ways
ingredients:
1.8kg taro
6 tablespoons olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
4 onions
6 celery sticks
6 carrots
4 flat-leaf parsley sprigs
2 heaped tablespoons tomato purée
1 × 400g tin of plum tomatoes
1 lemon
750g taro
1.2 litres vegetable stock
6 garlic cloves
400g Swiss chard
1 bunch of coriander
½ bunch of dill
5 tablespoons olive oil
1 heaped teaspoon ground coriander
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 lemon
steps:
Peel the taro. Now, you don’t want to cut it, you want to break the flesh. Insert a sharp knife no more than halfway into the taro, then carefully put pressure on it and twist a little so that the taro cracks. Repeat this with the taro pieces, so you create smaller pieces – you are looking for 4–5cm chunks. Place the olive oil in a large saucepan or flameproof casserole over a medium heat. Fry the taro chunks for about 15 minutes, seasoning them as they fry and turning so they are golden all over (you will probably have to do this in batches).
While the taro is frying, prepare the rest of the vegetables. Peel and chop the onions. Trim and cut the celery in 1–1.5cm slices. Roughly chop any little pale leaves from the inside the celery, if you have the heart. Peel and slice the carrots to a similar thickness. When the taro has all been fried, place in a bowl and reduce the heat under the pan a little. Add all the chopped vegetables and whole parsley sprigs to the pan and sauté for 15 minutes. When they are looking sticky, stir in the tomato purée and fry for a couple more minutes. Add the tomatoes to the pan and break them up with a wooden spoon. Add enough water to the pan to just cover all the vegetables, squeeze in the juice from the lemon, season well and stir. Bring to the boil, then cover the pan, reduce the heat to low, and cook for 45–60 minutes. The taro needs to be tender but you don’t want the pieces to be falling apart. When it is ready, remove the lid, turn the heat up and reduce the sauce a little. Taste and tweak the seasoning as needed, then leave to cool a little before serving.
Peel the taro and break it, don’t cut it. Insert a sharp knife no more than halfway into the taro, then carefully put pressure on it and twist a little so that the taro cracks. Repeat until you have 2–3cm chunks.
When you are ready to cook, place the stock in a large saucepan over a high heat and bring to the boil.
Peel and finely chop the garlic. Trim and finely slice the chard. Trim the herbs and finely chop them, stalks and all. Place another large saucepan or frying pan on a medium-low heat and add the olive oil and garlic. Sauté for 2 minutes until lightly golden, then add the ground coriander, and then all the sliced chard and half of the chopped herbs. Season generously with salt and pepper, then fry for 25 minutes, until the greens have cooked down and darkened.
When the greens are ready, rinse the taro and place into the boiling stock. Cook for about 15 minutes over a medium heat, or until tender, then stir in the cooked greens. Add the remaining chopped herbs and squeeze in the juice of the lemon. Taste, adjust the seasoning, and serve.

title: Shchi: cabbage and caraway soup
ingredients:
2 onions
4 garlic cloves
1 leek
2 carrots
400g waxy potatoes
500g white cabbage
4 tablespoons sunflower oil
2 tablespoons tomato purée
1 teaspoon caraway seeds
¼ teaspoon sweet smoked paprika
1.5 litres vegetable stock
2 bay leaves
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
½ bunch of dill
steps: Peel and finely chop the onions and garlic. Trim and finely slice the leek, then rinse it well in a colander to get rid of any dirt. Peel the carrots and potatoes, the chop them into 2cm pieces, keeping them separate. Halve the cabbage, remove the core, and finely shred the leaves. Place the sunflower oil in a large casserole or saucepan over a medium-low heat. Add the onions, garlic, leek and carrots and sauté for 15 minutes, until softened and sticky. Stir in the tomato purée, caraway seeds and paprika, then after a minute add the shredded cabbage, chopped potato, vegetable stock and bay leaves. Turn up the heat and bring to the boil. Season generously, then reduce the heat to a simmer. Cook on a low heat for 1 hour, until the vegetables are tender and the broth is rich. Taste and tweak the seasoning. Leave for 10 minutes before serving. Finely chop the dill, then ladle the soup into bowls and serve scattered with dill, and a slice of rye bread on the side.

title: Pepper-braised cabbage wedges
ingredients:
1 white cabbage, around 900g
5 tablespoons sunflower oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
3 onions
1 red pepper
2 tablespoons tomato purée
½ teaspoon sweet paprika
1 × 400g tin of plum tomatoes
1 tablespoon caster sugar
1 bay leaf
300ml hot vegetable stock
1 lemon
50g walnuts, optional
steps:
Trim the cabbage, removing any tatty outer leaves, and cut into eight wedges. Cut out a little of the thick core, but leaving a little in place to hold the leaves together (having said that if they fall apart it isn’t the end of the world – just makes them harder to fry). Place a wide flameproof casserole or large frying pan on a medium heat and add three tablespoons of sunflower oil. Season and fry the cut sides of the cabbage wedges for around 8 –10 minutes, turning halfway through, until charred – this will give it amazing flavour overall. While the cabbage is searing, peel and finely slice the onions. Halve the pepper, remove the seeds, and finely slice. When the cabbage is ready, keep to one side, turn the heat down a little and sauté the sliced onions and pepper for 10 minutes, adding the remaining 2 tablespoons of sunflower oil and seasoning them well. When they are soft, add the tomato purée and sweet paprika to the pan, fry for a couple of minutes then add the plum tomatoes, sugar, bay leaf and stock. Bring to the boil, breaking the tomatoes up with your wooden spoon, and season well. Once the sauce is boiling, gently nestle in the cabbage wedges, cut side up, and squeeze over the juice of half of the lemon. Season, cover the pan with a lid and reduce the heat to low. Cook for 45 minutes, until the cabbage is tender.
Meanwhile, if using the walnuts, preheat your oven to 180°C/fan 160°C/gas mark 4. Place the walnuts in a small ovenproof dish and toast in the oven for 8 minutes. Leave to cool then roughly chop. When the cabbage is ready, remove the lid from the pan, stir in the chopped walnuts and turn the heat up. Cook for a further 10 –12 minutes, so that the sauce has reduced and is thickened. Taste, adjust the seasoning and squeeze in lemon juice to taste.

title: Erene’s nistisimo keftedes
ingredients:
4 baking potatoes, around 700g
2 carrots
1 onion
1 courgette
2 plum tomatoes
½ bunch of flat-leaf parsley
200g dried breadcrumbs
½ × 400g tin of chopped tomatoes
1 tablespoon fine sea salt
1 tablespoon dried mint
½ tablespoon ground black pepper
1–1.5 litres vegetable oil, for frying
Flaky sea salt, to finish
steps:
Using a box grater or a food processor, grate the potatoes and carrots through the small holes. Peel the onion, then grate it, the courgette and tomatoes using the coarse side of the grater, or a larger food processor attachment. Finely chop the parsley, stalks and leaves. As each vegetable is grated, place into your largest mixing bowl, then add all the remaining ingredients, except the oil. Using your hands, mix everything together until evenly combined. Set the bowl aside for 15 minutes.
Get some trays ready: you’ll need a couple for the uncooked keftedes and a couple that are lined with kitchen paper, ready for the cooked ones. Place the oil in a large deep pan – you want it to be at least 6cm deep – and place on a high heat. While it is heating, shape the keftedes. Take a small amount, about a heaped tablespoon, in your hand, squeeze it a little to discard any extra moisture and shape into balls, or use the natural curve of your palm to shape into rounded oblongs. Shape all the mixture, placing the keftedes on the trays as you go.
When the oil is hot, about 170°C, carefully place the keftedes in the oil, about six at a time, depending on the size of your pan. Once they have a bit of colour, you can give them a gentle stir or prod, in case they need help releasing from the bottom of the pan – don’t do it too soon or they will fall apart. When they are a nice brown colour, after about 4 minutes, remove from the pan to the kitchen paper-lined trays to absorb the oil, and sprinkle with flaky salt. Repeat with the remaining mixture, then serve and eat.

title: Manitaria stifado: wild mushrooms, onions and garlic in wine
ingredients:
600g very small or baby onions
1kg wild mushrooms
4 garlic cloves
4 tablespoons olive oil
1 teaspoon ground allspice
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
4 thyme sprigs
3 bay leaves
1 cinnamon stick
200ml red wine
200ml tomato passata
2 tablespoons red wine vinegar
steps:
Bring a large pan of water to the boil. Remove from the heat and add the unpeeled onions to the pan. Leave for 2 minutes, then remove. This will make them easier to peel, which you want to do carefully, leaving them whole if possible. Trim and wipe the mushrooms clean, tearing any large ones in half. Peel and finely slice the garlic.
Preheat your oven to 200°C/fan 180°C/gas mark 6. Place a large flameproof casserole on a medium-low heat and add the olive oil and peeled onions. Fry for 5 minutes then add the sliced garlic and allspice. Fry slowly for another 5 minutes, just so that everything is lightly golden. Add the wild mushrooms to the pan, season well, pick in the thyme leaves and fry for 5–10 more minutes – until the mushrooms have released their moisture and start to become golden. Don’t stir them too often, allow them to get some colour from the pan. Add the bay leaves, cinnamon stick and red wine to the pan and turn up the heat. Bring to the boil and let it all bubble for a couple of minutes to reduce the wine a little. Add the passata and red wine vinegar and bring to the boil again, and then cover the casserole with a lid. Transfer to the oven and cook for 35 minutes, removing the lid for the last 15 minutes, until the onions are soft and the sauce is rich and reduced.

title: Alissa’s borscht
ingredients:
6 garlic cloves
1 onion
1 carrot
Sunflower oil
6 red beetroots
2 red peppers
2 tablespoons tomato purée
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
2 bay leaves
1 tablespoon black peppercorns
1 tablespoon coriander seeds
1 tablespoon fennel seeds
1 bunch of dill
½ bunch of flat-leaf parsley
500g sauerkraut
2 tablespoons pomegranate molasses
1 red onion
1 tablespoon brown sugar
1 × 400g tin of kidney beans
2 teaspoons sweet smoked paprika
steps:
Peel the garlic. Peel and finely chop the onion. Peel and grate the carrot. Pour a tablespoon of sunflower oil into a large saucepan and fry the onion and carrot over a medium heat for 8 minutes, until softened and the onion is golden. While that’s happening, peel and grate two of the beetroots. Halve one of the peppers, remove the seeds and finely slice the flesh. Add that all to the pan with the onions, then stir in the tomato purée and a splash of water. Season well, and fry for a further 5–8 minutes. When it has all started to soften, pour over 2 litres of water and add the bay leaves, peppercorns, coriander seeds, fennel seeds, four of the peeled garlic cloves and half of the dill and half of the flat-leaf parsley. Season with a tablespoon of salt and bring to the boil. Reduce the heat, finely grate in the remaining two garlic cloves and add half the sauerkraut with its brine and simmer, covered, over a low heat for 1 hour. Turn off the heat and let the borscht rest for another hour or so, while you prepare the rest of the elements.
Here is where the recipe starts to deviate from tradition quite a lot: to prepare the vegetables that will grace the plate and also add extra flavour and texture to the soup, you will need to do a bit of roasting. Preheat your oven to 180°C/fan 160°C/gas mark 4. Peel the remaining four beetroot, then cut them into wedges and place in a roasting tray. Drizzle with sunflower oil, season with salt and the pomegranate molasses. Peel the red onion, cut into thin wedges and season with salt and the brown sugar to bring out its sweetness. Place in the roasting tray with the beetroot and roast together for 30 minutes. Drain the kidney beans, then dress them with salt, oil and the smoked paprika. Core and deseed the remaining pepper, then cut into thin strips and dress with salt and oil. Roast the beans and pepper together in a roasting tray, as they will need only 10–15 minutes.
When all the vegetables are ready, strain the broth through a fine sieve or a muslin cloth, discarding the solids. Reheat the broth. Next create layers of texture and flavour in each bowl by adding a heaped tablespoon of the remaining sauerkraut to each, as well as a handful of roasted beetroot, onion, kidney beans and red pepper. Top each bowl with the hot broth. Chop the remaining dill and flat-leaf parsley, and sprinkle over the top. Serve with a spoon of dairy-free sour cream, or regular, if you prefer.

title: Prassinopita: celebration of greens pie
ingredients:
400g strong white bread flour, plus a little extra
2 teaspoons fine sea salt
1 tablespoon caster sugar
½ × 7g sachet of fast-action dried yeast
Olive oil
1 medium courgette, around 200g
1 leek
4 spring onions
200g baby leaf spinach
¼ teaspoon fennel seeds
1 bunch of dill
½ bunch of flat-leaf parsley
1 teaspoon freshly ground white pepper
1 lemon
2 tablespoons sesame seeds
3 tablespoons honey (or agave syrup)
steps:
Place the strong white bread flour in a large mixing bowl (or the bowl of a free standing mixer) and whisk in one teaspoon of the fine sea salt. In a jug mix together the caster sugar and yeast with 225ml of warm water. Leave for a few minutes. Use your fingers to rub in four tablespoons of olive oil to the flour (or use a dough hook), then make a well in the middle. Mix in the yeast water, adding a few more tablespoons of water if the dough needs it to come together – you don’t want it to be dry. Turn out the dough on a lightly floured surface, and knead for 8–10 minutes, until smooth and elastic. Alternatively use a free-standing mixer with a dough hook to do this for you. Transfer the kneaded dough to a clean, lightly oiled bowl and leave to prove for 1 hour.
While the dough is proving, prepare the filling. Trim and slice the courgette lengthways, the finely slice each half. Trim and slice the leek in the same way, then place the finely sliced leek in a colander and rinse thoroughly to remove any grit. Trim and finely slice the spring onions. Place them all in a large colander with the baby leaf spinach and scrunch in the remaining teaspoon of fine salt, really turning the vegetables. Leave the colander in the sink for 30 minutes, scrunching it all together again halfway through.
Preheat your oven to 220°C/fan 200°C/gas mark 7. Grind the fennel seeds using a pestle and mortar. Finely chop the dill and flat-leaf parsley. Scrunch the filling in the colander one last time and really squeeze out the excess liquid – it should look as if the greens have been wilted down and cooked slightly. Transfer to a large mixing bowl. Add the chopped dill and parsley, the white pepper and the juice from the lemon, and mix through the greens with your hand.
Turn the dough out to a lightly floured work surface and pat into a ball. Roll or push the dough out into a circle, about 35cm diameter, and heap the salted greens in the middle of the dough. Bring the sides up over the filling and join them together in the middle so you have a big pie. Drizzle a little oil into a 24cm ovenproof frying pan and carefully transfer the pie to the pan, patting and easing it in, seam-side down, so it fills the pan. Drizzle the top of the pie with a little more olive oil and pat on the sesame seeds and ground fennel seeds. Place the pan on a medium heat and fry for 2–3 minutes, or until it starts to sizzle, then transfer the pan to the oven. Bake for 25–30 minutes, or until golden all over. Remove the pie from the oven and drizzle with the honey. Leave to stand for 5 minutes before serving warm – it’s also really nice at room temperature.

title: Mushroom, potato and cumin bourekia
ingredients:
500g chestnut mushrooms
1 onion
2 garlic cloves
1 waxy potato, about 200g
4 thyme sprigs
5 tablespoons olive oil, plus extra for the trays
Sea salt flakes and freshly ground black pepper
½ teaspoon ground cumin
2 × 320g sheets of dairy-free puff pastry
steps:
Trim and wipe clean the mushrooms, then chop into 1cm pieces. Peel and finely chop the onion and garlic cloves. Peel and coarsely grate the potato. Pick the thyme leaves. Place a large frying pan over a medium heat and add three tablespoons of olive oil. Add the mushrooms, onion, garlic and thyme leaves. Season well with half a teaspoon of sea salt and quarter of a teaspoon of freshly ground black pepper, and fry for 15 minutes. Halfway through, stir in the grated potato and ground cumin. The filling is ready when the mushrooms have released their moisture and started to turn golden, and the potato is just tender. Turn off the heat and leave the filling to cool.
When you are ready to make the bourekia, preheat your oven to 220°C/fan 200°C/gas mark 7. Grease two baking trays with a little oil. Have a small bowl of cold water to hand. Unroll the puff pastry sheets and cut out 20 circles that are 9cm in diameter. You may need to cut and smooth together the edges of some of the trimmings to get the last couple of circles on each sheet. Spoon a heaped dessert spoon of the mushroom mixture into the centre of each circle of pastry. Dip your finger in the cold water and run around the edge of the pastry and fold half over to enclose the filling, creating a semi-circle shape. Pinch the edge of the pastry together, then use a fork to press the join firmly together. Place the pies on the greased baking trays and brush the tops of each with a little oil and sprinkle with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Bake for 18–22 minutes, or until golden and risen. Leave the pies to cool for at least 5 minutes on the tray before eating them.

title: Kolokithopita: pumpkin and raisin pie with harissa
ingredients:
800g pumpkin or butternut squash
125ml olive oil
1 teaspoon sea salt
Freshly ground black pepper
1 teaspoon ground cinnamon
1½ tablespoons harissa paste
1 tablespoon caster sugar
40g fine bulgur wheat
50g sultanas or raisins
4 spring onions
½ bunch of dill
300g filo pastry
1 garlic clove
steps:
Preheat the oven to 240°C/fan 220°C/gas mark 9. Peel and chop the pumpkin into 2cm pieces and place in a roasting tray with three tablespoons of the olive oil, half a teaspoon of sea salt, a good pinch of freshly ground black pepper, the ground cinnamon, one tablespoon of the harissa paste and the sugar. Toss together well, spread out into one even layer and pop in the oven for 25–30 minutes, until the pumpkin is charred around the edges. Remove from the oven, spoon into a bowl and leave to cool. When the pumpkin has cooled, stir in the bulgur wheat and sultanas or raisins. Trim and finely chop the spring onions and dill. Add all the spring onions and half of the dill to the bowl and mix everything together, crushing and mashing the pumpkin pieces down a bit.
When ready to bake, preheat your oven to 220°C/fan 200°C/gas mark 7. Brush a 22cm springform cake tin with a little oil. Lay out a sheet of filo, longest side nearest to you, and brush with oil, then top with another sheet. Spoon one-third of the mixture in a line about 4cm above the bottom edge of the pastry, then brush the pastry with more oil. Roll the pastry and filling up like a cigar then curl it into a swirl; this is the centre of your pie. Place the filled swirl in the middle of the cake tin. Repeat the filling and rolling process with the remaining sheets of filo and filling, adding each length to the pie spiral, so you have a coiled snake effect. Brush the entire pie with a little more oil and sprinkle with the remaining salt. Bake for 35–45 minutes, until crisp and deep golden brown.
While the pie is baking, make the finishing oil. Crush the garlic, in its skin, with the side of your knife and place in a small pan with four tablespoons of olive oil. Gently fry over a low heat, until it starts smelling wonderful but it doesn’t burn – about 4 minutes. Remove the pan from the heat and immediately stir in the remaining half-tablespoon of harissa. Leave to cool. When the pie is ready, brush with the harissa garlic oil, discarding the garlic clove, and leave the pie to stand for at least 15 minutes. Serve sprinkled with the remaining chopped dill.
source: The Secret to Delicious Vegan Cooking from the Mediterranean and Beyond.epub

title: Father Augustine’s kebbet laktin
ingredients:
1kg pumpkin or butternut squash, or 400g pumpkin purée
1 onion
250g fine bulgur wheat
½ teaspoon ground cinnamon
¼ teaspoon ground allspice
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
3 tablespoons plain flour
100ml olive oil
5 red onions
2 garlic cloves
200g baby leaf spinach
1 teaspoon cumin seeds
½ teaspoon pul biber or dried chilli flakes
3 tablespoons pomegranate molasses
2 tablespoons toasted pine nuts
steps:
If you are using fresh pumpkin, peel and deseed the pumpkin, then chop the flesh into 3cm chunks. Place the pumpkin in a large pan, cover with water and bring to the boil over a high heat. Reduce to a simmer and cook until the flesh is tender, 20–30 minutes. Drain in a colander and leave to steam dry for 30 minutes so that all the excess liquid evaporates. Peel and finely chop the onion and set aside.
Once the pumpkin is cooled and dry, you should have around 400g. Transfer to a large mixing bowl and blitz to a purée with a stick blender. Stir in the chopped onion, fine bulgur wheat, cinnamon and allspice, and season with a quarter-teaspoon each of salt and pepper. Leave the mixture to one side for 30 minutes, so the bulgur wheat has a chance to absorb the moisture from the pumpkin. Stir in the plain flour till combined, then use your hands to knead the mixture until you have a smooth dough. If the mixture is looking dry and crumbly, very gradually add enough water to bring it together – depending on the pumpkin you may need to add up to six tablespoons. This is OK, just keep going slowly until it all comes together.
Preheat your oven to 220°C/fan 200°C/gas mark 7. Brush a deep, loose-bottomed 24cm fluted pie tin with a little oil (I find larger flutes work better with this recipe). Press the pumpkin-bulgur dough evenly into the base and up the sides of the tin. Drizzle generously with olive oil, and gently brush it round so that everything is covered; brush up the fluted edge, or tilt the tin, so that the outer crust has a slick of oil too. Place the tin in the oven and bake for about 35 minutes, until the crust is golden all over and the top of the edge is slightly browned.
While the crust is cooking, make the filling. Peel and finely slice the red onions and garlic. Rinse the spinach well, and set aside to drain. Place a wide pan on a medium-low heat and add three tablespoons of the olive oil. Add the sliced onions and garlic and cook for 10 minutes, covered, until they have started to soften. Stir in the cumin seeds, pul biber and a teaspoon each of sea salt and freshly ground black pepper. Fry for a further 15 minutes, with the lid off, stirring occasionally, until sticky and sweet. Stir in the pomegranate molasses and cook for a further 5 minutes – the onions should be gloriously pink. Add the spinach, turn up the heat a little and cook for 8–10 minutes, until all the leaves have wilted and there is hardly any moisture left in the pan. When both the filling and crust are ready, spoon the filling into the case. Remove from the tin and slide onto a serving board. Finish by sprinkling over the pine nuts and leave to stand for 5 minutes before serving.

title: Revithosoup: houmous soup
ingredients:
2 onions
1 carrot
2 celery sticks
4 tablespoons olive oil, plus extra to serve
500g cooked chickpeas or jarred/tinned chickpeas (drained weight, liquid reserved)
1 garlic clove
4 tablespoons tahini
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
1–2 lemons
A few flat-leaf parsley sprigs
Sweet smoked paprika, to taste
2 tablespoons toasted sesame seeds
steps:
Peel and chop the onions and carrot. Trim and chop the celery. Place a large saucepan on a medium-low heat and add the olive oil and chopped vegetables. Sauté for 15 minutes, until the vegetables are starting to soften and become sticky and sweet, then add the chickpeas and 500ml of cooking water (or any liquid from the jar or tin, if using). Bring to the boil, then reduce the heat to a simmer and cook for 20 minutes.
When the soup mixture has cooked for 20 minutes, peel and roughly chop the garlic clove and add to the pan along with the tahini and generous pinch of salt and pepper. Blitz with a stick blender, until smooth and creamy. Squeeze in the juice of one lemon, stir and taste. Tweak the seasoning by adding more lemon, salt and pepper to taste. Depending on what chickpeas you used (and if you used any chickpea liquid) you may need to add an additional 100–250ml of just-boiled water to reach a consistency you like. Pick and finely chop the parsley leaves. Serve the soup in bowls, finished with a drizzle of olive oil and the chopped parsley scattered, plus a sprinkle of paprika and toasted sesame seeds.

title: Roasted squash, lentil and coriander soup
ingredients:
1 small butternut squash, around 750g
2 red onions
3 tablespoons olive oil
1 teaspoon ground coriander
½ teaspoon ground cumin
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
2 litres vegetable stock
1 teaspoon ground turmeric
75g red lentils
½ lemon
A few coriander sprigs
steps:
Preheat your oven to 210°C/fan 190°C/gas mark 6½. Trim and peel the butternut squash. Cut in half, remove the seeds, then cut into 3cm chunks. Peel the onions and cut into large wedges. Place the vegetables in a large roasting tray, drizzle over the olive oil, then sprinkle with the ground coriander, ground cumin and a good pinch of salt and pepper, and toss to combine. Place in the oven and roast for around 45 minutes, or until the squash is cooked through and caramelised around the edges.
Meanwhile, pour three-quarters of the stock into a large saucepan and add the turmeric and lentils. Bring to the boil over a high heat, then reduce to a simmer and cook for 25 minutes. When the squash and onions are ready, scrape them into the saucepan with the lentils and simmer for a further 5 minutes. Blitz the soup with a stick blender until mostly smooth – a bit of texture is nice. Add the extra stock, if you prefer it thinner, and bring the soup back to a simmer. Just before you are ready to eat, squeeze in the juice from the lemon half, then taste and tweak the seasoning. Roughly chop the coriander and sprinkle over the top before serving.

title: Kibbet el raheb: monks’ soup
ingredients:
1 shallot or small onion
100g plain flour
75g fine bulgur wheat
½ teaspoon ground allspice
½ teaspoon ground cinnamon
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
6 mint sprigs
½ bunch of flat-leaf parsley
Olive or vegetable oil
2 garlic cloves
2 red onions
250g spinach or Swiss chard
150g brown lentils
2 tablespoons pomegranate molasses
½ lemon
steps:
Peel and chop the shallot as finely as you can and place in a bowl with the flour, bulgur wheat, allspice, cinnamon and a quarter-teaspoon each of salt and pepper. Pick the mint and parsley leaves and finely chop them together, then add half to the bowl and set the rest aside. Add 6 tablespoons of cold water, then use your hands to bring the mixture all together until you have a firm dough. Knead in the bowl for 5 minutes until the dough is consistently smooth then roll into 2cm balls and lay out on a tray. You should get about 45 little dumplings.
Place a large saucepan on a medium-low heat and add four tablespoons of oil. Fry the dumplings for around 12–15 minutes, turning, until lightly browned all over. You will probably need to do this in batches. Spoon the browned dumplings back on to the tray and keep to one side.
Peel the garlic and red onions and finely slice. Add them both to the pan with a little more oil and fry for 15 minutes or so, until golden brown. Wash the spinach or chard, trim the ends and roughly slice the leaves and finely slice the stems, then add it all to the pan with the lentils and pomegranate molasses. Stir for a minute then cover with 1.5 litres of cold water and turn up the heat. Bring to the boil, then cover, reduce the heat and simmer for 30 minutes. Add the dumplings back to the pan and cook for a further 20 minutes. Just before you want to serve, squeeze in the lemon juice, stir in the remaining chopped herbs and adjust the seasoning to taste.

title: Rishta: lentil and pasta soup
ingredients:
200g green lentils
1.8 litres hot vegetable stock
2 onions
4 garlic cloves
4 tablespoons olive oil
1 bunch of coriander
1 teaspoon cumin seeds
1 teaspoon ground coriander
125g tagliatelle
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
½ lemon
steps:
Rinse the lentils thoroughly under running water, and pick out any stones. Place in a large pan with the hot stock and bring to the boil. Reduce the heat to low and simmer for 45 minutes. Meanwhile, peel and finely slice the onions and garlic. Place a large frying pan over a medium-low heat and add the olive oil and sliced vegetables. Sauté for 15 minutes, until softened and just coloured. Finely chop the coriander. Stir the cumin seeds and ground coriander in with the onion and fry for a minute. Stir in half the fresh coriander to the frying pan, fry for a further 2 minutes, then remove from the heat.
When the lentils are ready, stir in the sautéed onion mixture. Roughly break the tagliatelle into smaller pieces and add to the soup. Season generously with salt and pepper and bring back to the boil. Reduce the heat and simmer for a further 5 minutes, or until the tagliatelle is just cooked. Squeeze in the juice of the lemon half and finish with the remaining chopped coriander before serving.

title: Fava, pickled onions and capers
ingredients:
300g dried yellow split peas
2 onions
2 garlic cloves
5 tablespoons extra virgin olive oil
4 rosemary sprigs
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 bay leaf
1 red onion
2 lemons
2 tablespoons capers
steps:
Place the yellow split peas in a sieve and rinse under running water. Peel and finely chop the onions and garlic. Place a large saucepan on a medium-low heat, pour in three tablespoons of olive oil and add the chopped vegetables to the pan. Pick in the rosemary leaves, season, and gently sauté the onion mixture for 10 minutes until soft and sticky but not coloured. Stir in the washed split peas and the bay leaf and pour in 1 litre of boiling water. Turn the heat up, bring it all to the boil then reduce the heat to low and cover with a lid. Cook gently for about 40 minutes, until the water has all been absorbed and the fava is thick and creamy. Periodically check during cooking and spoon off any white scum that comes to the surface, topping up with more boiling water if needed – don’t let it cook dry as it needs to be creamy.
While the fava is cooking, peel and finely slice the red onion. Squeeze over the juice of half a lemon, and leave to one side to soften.
When the fava is ready, discard the bay leaf, season generously and use a stick blender to blitz to a smooth purée. Squeeze in the juice from the remaining 1½ lemons and pour in a couple of tablespoons of extra virgin olive oil. Check the seasoning and beat it all together. Serve the creamy fava topped with dressed sliced onions and the capers.

title: Black-eyed beans, chard and lemon
ingredients:
250g dried black-eyed beans, or 2 × 400g jars/tins of beans
2 onions
2 garlic cloves
1 leek
200g Swiss chard
75ml olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
2 lemons
½ bunch of flat-leaf parsley
A few dill sprigs
steps:
Wash the dried black-eyed beans and remove any that don’t look good. Place in a large pan of cold water and bring to the boil. Cook for 50–60 minutes, or until just tender.
While the beans are cooking, peel and finely slice the onions and garlic. Trim, wash and finely slice the leek. Trim and slice the chard stalks, and roughly chop the leaves. Place a second large pan on a medium heat and add the olive oil. Fry the sliced onion, garlic, leeks and chard stalks for 15 minutes, until starting to soften, then add the chard leaves and cook for a further 5 minutes. When the black-eyed beans are ready, or if you’re using jarred or tinned beans, strain and add to the pan with the vegetables. Cover with just enough fresh water to cover and season well. Bring to the boil, then reduce the heat a little and simmer for 15 minutes with the lid on, then remove the lid and turn the heat up and cook for a further 5 minutes to reduce the liquid. The beans should be tender and there should be just enough liquid to loosen them, but it shouldn’t be soupy. Squeeze in the juice of one lemon to taste, then taste before adding any more. Finely chop the herbs and stir them in, then taste to check the seasoning before serving.

title: Prebranac: caramelised-onion baked beans
ingredients:
500g dried butter beans, or 4 × 400g jars/tins of butter beans, drained and liquid reserved
1 bay leaf
6 onions
8 garlic cloves
100ml sunflower or olive oil
1 tablespoon sweet paprika
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
A few flat-leaf parsley sprigs, optional
steps:
If you are cooking the beans from scratch, first soak the dried beans for about 12 hours in plenty of cold water. After that time, drain the beans and place them in a large saucepan with the bay leaf. Cover with three times as much water and place the pan on a high heat. Bring to the boil, then reduce the heat and simmer for about 1½ hours, or until the beans are tender. Do not let them boil dry. Drain the cooked beans, reserving the cooking liquid.
Preheat the oven to 200°C/fan 180°C/gas mark 6. While the beans are cooking, peel and finely slice the onions and garlic. Place the oil in a large flameproof casserole or ovenproof pan and add the sliced onions. Sauté the onions slowly over a medium-low heat for about 30 minutes, until golden and sticky. If the onions start to catch even a little, add a splash of water. Add the sliced garlic and paprika for the final 10 minutes. Stir in the drained beans, 750ml of the cooking liquid (or liquid from the jars/tins) and season generously. If you need to, make up the amount of liquid with just-boiled water from a kettle. Place the uncovered casserole in the oven and cook for around 1–1½ hours. Check the beans a couple of times during cooking and add a splash more cooking liquid (or water from the kettle) if the dish looks like it is drying out. The end result should be golden on top, with soft and oozy beans underneath. Remove the casserole from the oven and set aside to let the beans cool, to serve warm or at room temperature. Finish by roughly chopping the parsley, if using, and scattering over the top, then serve with crusty bread. The beans are even better reheated the next day, or day after.

title: Lobio: spiced kidney beans, walnuts and coriander
ingredients:
400g dried kidney beans or 3 × 400g jars/tins of beans
2 bay leaves
3 onions
120g walnuts
1 large bunch of coriander
4 garlic cloves
½ teaspoon dill seeds, optional
¼ teaspoon cayenne pepper
1 teaspoon ground coriander
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 pomegranate
4 tablespoons olive oil
3 tablespoons pomegranate molasses
Extra virgin olive oil
steps:
Soak the dried kidney beans overnight in plenty of cold water. When you are ready to cook them, drain, and place in a large saucepan with the bay leaves and cover with plenty of fresh cold water. Bring to the boil then simmer for 1–1½ hours, until the beans are very tender.
Meanwhile, peel the onions. Finely chop two and a half of them, and finely slice the remaining onion half. Finely chop or grind the walnuts. Trim the coriander stalks and finely chop the stalks and leaves. Peel the garlic. Place the garlic in a mortar with the dill seeds (if using), cayenne pepper and ground coriander and quarter of a teaspoon each of salt and pepper. Grind until you have a creamy texture, then add two-thirds of the chopped coriander and pound that in too. Halve the pomegranate and carefully pick the seeds, and keep to one side.
Pour the olive oil into a large saucepan and sauté the chopped onions for 15 minutes over a medium-low heat, until cooked through and slightly golden. When the beans are ready, drain in a colander (reserving a large mugful of the cooking liquid) and return them to the warm pan. If you are using jarred or tinned beans, start with this step. Season generously, then use a wooden spoon, or even a potato masher to crush them so they break down. Spoon them into the pot with the onions and add the chopped walnuts, the garlicky spice paste, one tablespoon of the pomegranate molasses and half the reserved cooking water. Mix and crush everything together well until creamy, and return the pan to the heat and cook for 5 minutes. Add the remaining cooking liquid if needed, so that the beans aren’t too dry, and taste to adjust the seasoning as necessary. Spoon the seasoned beans into a serving bowl. Finish by drizzling over the remaining pomegranate molasses and a good amount of extra virgin olive oil, then garnish with the reserved coriander, pomegranate seeds and onion slices.

title: Fasoles: slow-cooked beans and garden vegetables
ingredients:
500g dried white beans (white kidney, cannellini, haricot), or 4 × 400g jars/tins of beans
2 onions
4 carrots
4 celery sticks
1 leek
400g waxy potatoes, Cyprus ideally
100ml olive oil
2 heaped tablespoons tomato purée
5 flat-leaf parsley sprigs, plus extra, optional, for serving
2 bay leaves
Sea salt and finely ground black pepper
Extra virgin olive oil – to finish (this is important, please don’t leave this out)
steps:
Start the night before by soaking the dried beans in plenty of cold water.
The next day, peel and crudely chop the onions and carrots. Trim and slice the celery sticks and leek into pieces 1–1.5cm thick. The vegetables are to be celebrated, not just a base, so you don’t want to chop them finely. Rinse the leek slices thoroughly in a colander to get rid of any dirt. Peel the potatoes and cut into 3cm chunks. Place a large flameproof casserole or saucepan over medium-low heat and add the olive oil. Add the chopped onion, carrot, celery and leek to the pan and sauté for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until they’re losing moisture and turning sweet and starting to soften. Stir in the potatoes and tomato purée and fry for a couple of minutes. Boil a full kettle of water. Add the drained dried or tinned beans to the other vegetables. Pour in enough boiling water to cover everything by 2cm. Add the parsley sprigs, bay leaves and season generously with salt and pepper – around a teaspoon of each – and bring back to a boil. Cover the pan, reduce the heat to low and simmer for 2½ hours, until the beans are tender. Remove the lid, and if the beans are looking liquidy, turn the heat up and bubble away for about 15 minutes, so that the fasoles become creamy and the liquid reduces and thickens. Taste and add more seasoning as required. Ideally leave the beans to sit for a few hours before serving, or even better overnight, as they become more delicious with time. Serve with a drizzle of extra virgin olive oil and a gesture of chopped parsley, if you like.

title: Maghmour: aubergine and chickpea stew
ingredients:
2 large or 3 medium aubergines
3 onions
6 garlic cloves
100ml olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 heaped tablespoon tomato purée
½ teaspoon cayenne pepper or dried chilli flakes
1 × 400g tin of plum tomatoes
400g cooked, peeled chickpeas or 2 × 400g jars/tins of chickpeas, drained
½ tablespoon dried mint
steps: Trim the aubergines, and use a speed peeler to remove most of the skin, leaving a ‘striped’ effect, and then cut into 4cm chunks. Peel and chop the onions. Peel and finely chop the garlic. Line a plate with kitchen paper. Place a large flameproof casserole on a medium heat and add the olive oil. Fry the aubergine in batches, for 5 minutes each side, so that they become golden. Season generously with sea salt and black pepper while cooking. Spoon onto the paper-lined plate, and repeat until all the aubergine is fried. Add the chopped onion and garlic to the pan, reduce the heat a little and sauté for 15 minutes, until softened and caramelising. Then, stir in the tomato purée and cayenne pepper, fry for a minute then add the tinned tomatoes and break them up with a wooden spoon. Add 400ml of water and bring to the boil. Add the cooked, jarred or tinned chickpeas to the pan with the aubergine, then sprinkle over the dried mint and reduce the heat a little. Simmer for 30 minutes, until everything is combined, soft and thickened. Turn off the heat and leave to stand for at least 10 minutes before serving.

title: Ta’ameya: broad bean falafel
ingredients:
300g dried split fava beans
1 red onion
2 garlic cloves
1 bunch of flat-leaf parsley
½ bunch of coriander
1 heaped teaspoon ground coriander
1 teaspoon ground cumin
¾ teaspoon fine sea salt
1 teaspoon bicarbonate of soda
30g toasted sesame seeds
1 litre vegetable oil
Flaky sea salt
2 lemons
steps:
Start this recipe the night (or morning) before by soaking the fava beans in plenty of cold water. Let them soak for at least 8 hours.
To make the ta’ameya, peel and roughly chop the onion and garlic. Trim and roughly chop the flat-leaf parsley and coriander. Place them all in a mixing bowl along with the ground coriander, ground cumin and sea salt. Drain the fava beans in a colander, and gently dry with kitchen paper. Stir them through the chopped herb and veg mixture until well mixed in then spoon into the bowl of a food processor. Pulse until roughly chopped then add the bicarbonate of soda and continue to pulse until you get a consistent dough. You don’t want a fine paste, which is why it is important to pulse and not leave the motor running, otherwise it will be too fine. Line a large tray with greaseproof paper and use a tablespoon measure to scoop heaped balls of the mixture and place on the tray – they should be around the size of a ping pong ball. Sprinkle them with the toasted sesame seeds and lightly pat them down so they have evenly flattened surfaces on the top and bottom.
When ready to fry the ta’ameya, heat the oil in a large saucepan over a medium heat. While it heats, cut the lemons in wedges and get the pita, salad and other accompaniments ready. Line a large plate or shallow bowl with kitchen paper. Test the oil is ready by putting a small cube of potato or bread in it. When it is golden, the oil is hot enough; if you have a thermometer, you’re looking for the oil to be 165–175°C. Fry the patties in batches for 3–4 minutes, then flip over and fry for a further 1–2 minutes, until browned all over. Use tongs or a slotted spoon to transfer the ta’ameya to the kitchen paper to absorb the excess oil, and sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Serve straight away with all the trimmings, and wedges of lemon to squeeze over.

title: Azadouhi’s vospov kofte: spiced red lentil balls
ingredients:
3 onions
2 bunches of flat-leaf parsley
3 tablespoons olive oil, plus extra, optional, for the salad
200g red split lentils
200g fine bulgur wheat
1 teaspoon ground cumin
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
3 ripe tomatoes
½ teaspoon sumac
1 lemon, optional
steps:
Peel and finely chop the onions. Finely chop the flat-leaf parsley, stalks and all. Place a large saucepan on a medium-low heat and add the olive oil and one-third of the chopped onions. Fry for 15 minutes, or until golden and soft. Stir in the red split lentils and cover with 1.25 litres of water. Turn up the heat, bring to the boil, then reduce to a simmer and cook for 25 minutes, or until the lentils are very soft. Drain the lentils and onion in a sieve over a bowl, so that you remove most of the excess water but reserve it for when you start kneading. The vegetables don’t need to be bone dry, but they shouldn’t be sopping wet. Transfer the lentils and onions to a large mixing bowl, then stir in the fine bulgur wheat, half the remaining chopped onion, one-third of the chopped parsley, the ground cumin and a half-teaspoon each of sea salt and freshly ground black pepper. Mix together then knead with your hands to form a paste – add as much of the drained water as you need to get a smooth mixture; it shouldn’t be dry, and you may need to add all of the reserved liquid, and even a touch more from the tap. Keep kneading, then take a small ball of the mixture and form with your hands into a small, two-bite kofte. Leave the indents of your fingers on the mixture.
Halve the tomatoes and scoop out the seeds and flesh. Finely chop the flesh and mix in a small bowl with the remaining chopped onion and parsley. Add the sumac, season well and stir to combine.
To eat, take a kofte and press it into the salad to make it stick, mopping up some of the juices as you go, and eat together. Or, less fun, you can dress the salad with the juice of the lemon and a little olive oil, and place on a plate with the kofte, to eat with a fork.

title: Jewelled moutzentra
ingredients:
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
250g dried green or brown lentils
130g long grain rice
4 onions
3 garlic cloves
4 tablespoons olive or sunflower oil
1 teaspoon cumin seeds
½ pomegranate
1 bunch of flat-leaf parsley
50g toasted flaked almonds
50g dried sour cherries
½ lemon
steps:
Place a large pan of salted water on to boil. Thoroughly rinse the lentils in a sieve, picking out any stones, and then cook in the boiling water for 20 minutes, until almost cooked. Meanwhile, rinse the rice in a sieve, then add to the pan for a further 12 minutes, until perfectly cooked – the rice isn’t meant to be mushy (although if I am making it just for me, I do like it a little mushy and so add an extra 2 minutes). Drain the rice and lentils in a sieve or fine colander, and return to the hot pan to steam dry and keep fluffy.
While the lentils are cooking, peel and finely slice the onions and garlic. Place a large frying pan on a medium heat and pour in the oil. Sauté the onions, garlic, cumin and a good pinch of salt and pepper for 20 minutes, until deep golden brown. To encourage them, I cover the frying pan with a lid for 10 minutes, adding a splash of water if needed, then fry uncovered for 10 minutes. Stir occasionally. While that’s happening, pick the pomegranate seeds. Pick and roughly chop the flat-leaf parsley leaves, and toss them with the toasted flaked almonds, sour cherries and pomegranate seeds. Squeeze over the juice from the lemon half, and toss it all together. When the onions are ready, stir through the cooked lentils, check the seasoning and plate up. Garnish with the dressed fruits and nuts and serve.

title: Mushroom and caramelised onion pilaf
ingredients:
2 onions
2 garlic cloves
500g mixed mushrooms
4 tablespoons olive oil
15g dried wild mushrooms
50g vermicelli pasta
200g long grain rice
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 bunch of dill
1 lemon
40g toasted pine nuts
A few pinches of pul biber, optional
steps:
Peel and finely slice the onions and garlic. Wipe, trim and roughly slice the mushrooms. Place a large flameproof casserole or saucepan on a medium-low heat and drizzle in half of the olive oil. Stir in the onions and garlic and sauté for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until softened and a little coloured. While that’s happening, place the dried mushrooms in a measuring jug, cover with boiling water and leave to one side. When the onions are soft and golden, stir in the sliced fresh mushrooms. Break in the vermicelli pasta, so that you have small pieces around 2–3cm long, then stir in with the mushrooms and onions, and turn the heat up. Fry for 5 minutes, until everything takes on a little more colour. Meanwhile, remove the dried mushrooms from their soaking water, reserving it for later. Slice the dried mushrooms add them to the pan, then also add the rice and stir everything together well and season generously. Top the reserved mushroom soaking liquor with enough boiling water to bring it up to 800ml and pour into the pan with the rice mixture. Bring to the boil, then reduce the heat to very low and cover. Cook for 20–25 minutes, stirring only once or twice. Finely chop the dill and keep to one side.
The pilaf is ready when all the water has been absorbed. Remove the pan from the heat, and squeeze in the juice of the lemon. Stir in the dill, then taste and adjust the seasoning. Spoon on to a platter and finish with sprinklings of toasted pine nuts and pul biber, if using.
source: The Secret to Delicious Vegan Cooking from the Mediterranean and Beyond.epub

title: Gemista: roasted stuffed vegetables
ingredients:
4 onions
8 tomatoes
2 round courgettes, if you can get them, or red peppers
75ml olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
2 tablespoons tomato purée
250g medium grain rice (you can use a mixture of short and long grain, however paella rice is probably most similar to the Greek rice traditionally used)
2 teaspoons dried mint
1 teaspoon ground cinnamon
½ bunch of flat-leaf parsley
650ml hot vegetable stock
1 lemon
steps:
To get ahead, I prepare the onions the night before – they need time to cool down before you stuff them. Cut off the top and bottom and peel off the skin. Make a vertical slice in the onions, halfway into the centre, so that once they are boiled you can peel off the layers in one piece. Place the onions in a large saucepan and cover them with water. Bring to the boil over a medium heat and cook for 40 minutes, till tender throughout. Remove the onions from the water and leave to cool completely.
When you are ready to cook the gemista, slice the tops off the tomatoes and the courgettes (or peppers). Set the tops aside to use later, and scoop out the middle of the vegetables – be careful to not scoop out too much of the tomatoes or they will fall apart. Put the tomato filling in a bowl to one side, but discard the seeds from the courgettes or peppers. Arrange the prepped vegetable shells in a roasting tray, leaving space for the stuffed rolled onions too.
Separate the onion layers, carefully easing them off one by one – you probably only want the first four or five layers from each onion. Finely chop the central onion core. Pour three tablespoons of the olive oil in a wide saucepan over a medium-low heat and fry the chopped onions for 10 minutes. Add half a teaspoon each of sea salt and freshly ground black pepper to the fried onion, then stir in one tablespoon of tomato purée. After a minute, roughly chop the reserved tomato flesh and add it to the pan, then continue to cook until most of the juices have reduced and you are left with a just little liquid in the bottom of the pan (this will be soaked up by the rice). Stir in the rice, dried mint, ground cinnamon and season with salt and pepper. Finely chop the parsley, then stir into the mixture in the pan and leave it all to cool.
Preheat the oven to 190°C/fan 170°C/gas mark 5. Spoon the cooled filling into the hollow vegetables, filling them up about three-quarters, so there is room for the rice to expand. Lay the large cooked onion petals out in front of you and stuff those also, leaving a bit of room for growth. Tuck the edges under, so you have an ‘eye’ shape, and nestle them into the tray, seam side down. Dissolve the remaining tablespoon of tomato purée in the hot stock and whisk in the juice from the lemon. Pour some of the stock over the filled vegetables and the rest directly into the tray, so that it comes just over halfway up the sides of the tallest vegetables. It is important there is enough liquid, so if it is not high enough up the vegetables, top it up with hot water. Replace the tops of the vegetables, drizzle them with the remaining oil and then cover the tray with foil and place in the oven. Cook for 1 hour, then remove the foil, turn the heat up to 220°C/fan 200°C/gas mark 7 and cook for a further 20–25 minutes, until the outsides of the vegetables are slightly caramelised. You can serve these straight away, but gemista are better if left to cool a little, ideally 20–30 minutes. The flavours develop and the rice gets a chance to soak up any extra liquid in the tray. They’re even nicer the next day.
source: The Secret to Delicious Vegan Cooking from the Mediterranean and Beyond.epub

title: Dolmades
ingredients:
4 onions
80ml olive oil
5 tomatoes
1 heaped tablespoon tomato purée
275g medium grain rice (or a mixture of short and long grain)
1 tablespoon dried mint
½ teaspoon ground cinnamon
½ teaspoon each of sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
75g pine nuts, optional
1 bunch of flat-leaf parsley
A few dill sprigs
50 vine leaves
2 lemons
steps:
Peel and finely chop the onions. Place half of the oil in a wide saucepan over a medium-low heat and soften the onions for 15 minutes. Stir them occasionally, and add a splash of water if they begin to catch. Coarsely grate in four of the tomatoes, discarding the skins. Stir in the tomato purée and keep cooking until most of the juices have reduced, and you are left with a little liquid in the bottom of the pan (this will be soaked up by the rice). Stir in the rice, dried mint, cinnamon, salt, pepper and pine nuts, if using. Finely chop the parsley and dill and add those to the pan, then turn off the heat and leave to cool.
Bring a large pan of water to the boil. In batches, blanch the vine leaves in a pan of boiling water for just a minute. Transfer to a colander, as you continue. When they are all ready, set yourself up a conveyor belt of leaves, filling and pan. To fill them, lay a leaf out in front of you, textured side facing up, with the stalk closest to you. Spoon a couple of teaspoons of the rice mixture towards the bottom of the leaf, in the centre, and roll the bottom edge of the leaf over the filling once. Fold over each side, then keep rolling until the leaf has encased the filling. The amount of mixture you use will depend on the size of the leaf. Once you start you’ll find your rhythm. Repeat with all the leaves and filling.
Line the bottom of a large saucepan with any broken or leftover vine leaves. Layer up the rolled dolmades, so they are closely layered but not packed too tight (the rice will expand as it cooks). Coarsely grate the remaining tomato into 800ml of just-boiled boiled water. Squeeze in the juice from the lemons and whisk in with the remaining olive oil. Pour the seasoned water over the layered vine leaves. If they are not quite covered, add enough just-boiled water so they are just covered. Place an upturned heavy plate directly on top of the dolmades, cover the pan with a lid and place on a medium heat. Bring to a steady simmer, then reduce the heat and cook for 45 minutes, until most of the liquid has been absorbed and the dolmades are cooked through. Open one up to test – you are looking for sweet, sticky, tomatoey rice that is tender and done. Turn off the heat and leave, still covered, to rest for at least 15 minutes before serving.

title: Maqluba: upside-down layer cake
ingredients:
1 small cauliflower, around 450g
350g waxy potatoes, Cyprus if possible
3 red onions
Olive oil
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper
2 teaspoons Lebanese seven-spice (for how to make your own)
2 tablespoons pomegranate molasses
600g rice (see above)
3 large ripe tomatoes
1 large aubergine
200g vermicelli pasta or noodles
½ teaspoon dried oregano
800ml hot vegetable stock
40g pine nuts
40g flaked almonds
½ bunch of flat-leaf parsley
steps:
Preheat your oven to 220°C/fan 200°C/gas mark 7. Cut the cauliflower into even florets, halving any larger pieces. Slice the potatoes into 5mm-thick slices. Peel the onions and cut into 2cm-thick wedges. Place these all in a large roasting tray and drizzle liberally with olive oil. Season generously and sprinkle with the Lebanese seven-spice. Toss together and roast for 30 minutes, drizzling with the pomegranate molasses 5 minutes before the end, so that the vegetables lightly char and caramelise.
Meanwhile, prepare the rest of the ingredients. Boil a kettle and line a large plate and a small plate with kitchen paper. Place the rice in a large bowl and cover with just-boiled water and leave to one side. Slice the tomatoes into 1cm-thick slices. Trim the aubergines and slice into 1cm strips lengthways. Place a large frying pan on a medium heat and drizzle in enough olive oil to just cover the base of the pan. In batches, fry the aubergine for 8–10 minutes, turning halfway through and seasoning while cooking, until lightly golden all over. Transfer to the large paper-lined plate. Break the pasta (or noodles) into small pieces and place in the pan, still on a medium heat. Add another layer of oil and fry the pasta pieces for about 5 minutes, or until golden brown. Turn off the heat and transfer the pasta to the small paper-lined plate. Drain the rice in a sieve, then return to the bowl and toss through the fried vermicelli. Season with half a teaspoon each of salt and pepper.
Now, everything should be ready for you to layer up the maqluba. Line the base of a large saucepan with the fried aubergine slices, allowing them to come slightly up the side of the pan to help the maqluba maintain its structure. Next, lay over the tomato slices and sprinkle with oregano. Top with half of the roasted cauliflower and red onion wedges, arranged evenly. Place two-thirds of the rice-vermicelli mixture into the pan, patting it in to make it even. Top with the roasted potato and the remaining cauliflower and onion. Scatter over the remaining rice mixture. Pour in the hot stock. It should sit about 1cm under the level of the rice.
Put the pan on a medium heat and bring it the boil, then reduce the heat to the lowest setting. Place a thick plate, slightly smaller than the pan, on top, so that it sits directly on top of the rice, and cover the pan with a lid. Cook on a low heat for 1 hour and 15 minutes, until the rice is cooked through and the water has been absorbed. If it is not quite ready, cook for a further 10 minutes. Remove from the heat and leave to one side, still covered, for 10 minutes. Meanwhile, toast the pine nuts and flaked almonds in a small dry frying pan, stirring occasionally, over a low heat for 5 minutes, or until lightly golden. Finely chop the parsley leaves. When the maqluba has stood for 10 minutes, remove the lid and plate and place a wide, heavy platter on top of the pan. Quickly and confidently turn the pan over and give it a tap. The maqluba should turn out in one piece. Remove the pan, then scatter with the toasted nuts and parsley before taking to the table.

title: Spanakorizo: sweet and smoky spinach, tomato and lemon rice
ingredients:
2 onions
2 garlic cloves
1 leek
4 spring onions
75ml olive oil
1 heaped teaspoon smoked or regular flaky salt
400g spinach
200g long grain rice
2 tablespoons tomato purée
1 heaped teaspoon sugar
¼ teaspoon sweet smoked paprika
350ml tomato passata or 5 ripe tomatoes
750ml vegetable stock
Freshly ground black pepper
1 lemon
½ bunch of dill
steps:
Start by peeling and chopping the onions and garlic cloves. Trim and finely slice the leek and give it a thorough rinse in a colander to get rid of any dirt. Trim and slice the spring onions into 1cm pieces. Place the olive oil in a large saucepan over a medium-low heat. Add the chopped vegetables and smoked (or regular) salt and sauté for 15 minutes, until softened and sticky but not coloured. Meanwhile, really thoroughly wash the spinach – the last thing you want is grit in the spinach, so my yiayia always washes hers three times! When it is grit-free, roughly chop and leave to one side. Rinse the rice in a sieve under running water for minute.
When the vegetables are ready, stir in the tomato purée, sugar and sweet smoked paprika. Fry for a few minutes, then stir in the washed rice and cook for a further minute. Add the passata (or coarsely grate in the tomatoes, discarding the skin) and the stock, then season with a few pinches of pepper. Turn the heat up and bring to the boil. Once it is bubbling, stir in the chopped spinach, then cover with the lid and reduce the heat to low. Cook for 30 minutes, stirring once halfway through and adding more water if it looks like the rice has dried out and is sticking to the bottom of the pan. After half an hour, the rice should be cooked; give it a stir and check the texture – it should feel like a paella. If it is a little on the wet side, cook with the lid off to reduce it. Remember the rice will absorb liquid as it cools, so don’t reduce the liquid too much. Squeeze in the lemon juice, taste and tweak the seasoning, then leave for 5 minutes before serving. Finely chop the dill and scatter over the rice. Serve warm.

title: Milopita: apple, brown sugar and cinnamon cake
ingredients:
4 eating apples
Juice of ½ lemon, or a splash of brandy
200g light soft brown sugar
275g self-raising flour
1 teaspoon baking powder
100g ground almonds
2 teaspoons ground cinnamon
¼ teaspoon fine sea salt
200ml vegetable oil, plus extra for the tin
150ml almond milk
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
40g mixed nuts (walnuts, hazelnuts, almonds)
Icing sugar, to finish
steps: Preheat your oven to 190°C/fan 170°C/gas mark 5. Peel the apples and cut into quarters. Remove the core then finely slice the flesh. Place the apple slices in a large bowl, and toss with the lemon juice (or brandy) and 175g of the light soft brown sugar and leave for 5 minutes. Add the self-raising flour, baking powder, ground almonds, ground cinnamon and sea salt. Toss to combine, then add the vegetable oil, almond milk and vanilla, then mix together. Grease a 24cm round dish with a little oil. Spoon in the apple cake mixture. Roughly chop the nuts, then sprinkle them over the top with the remaining 25g of sugar. Place in the oven and bake for 40–45 minutes, or until golden and just cooked through. Dust with sifted icing sugar and leave to cool for 10 minutes before serving.

title: Sticky chocolate-orange pudding
ingredients:
80ml vegetable oil, plus extra for the tin
250g caster sugar
130g plain flour
2 teaspoons baking powder
55g cocoa powder
¼ teaspoon fine sea salt
3 oranges, or 1 orange and 125ml orange juice
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
75g light soft brown sugar
Icing sugar, to finish
steps:
Preheat your oven to 200°C/fan 180°C/gas mark 6. Grease a deep oval 25cm ceramic dish with a little oil.
In a large mixing bowl whisk together 150g of the caster sugar, the plain flour, the baking powder, 30g of the cocoa powder and the fine sea salt. Finely grate in the zest of one of the oranges and then whisk the dry ingredients all together. Finely grate, or pare and finely slice, the zest from another orange, and set aside. Squeeze the oranges into a jug to get 125ml of orange juice (alternatively, use 125ml of fresh orange juice). Whisk the vegetable oil and vanilla extract into the juice. Mix the wet mixture into the dry ingredients. Spoon the batter into the prepared baking dish and even out across the top. Put a kettle of water on to boil. In a medium mixing bowl, combine the light soft brown sugar with the remaining 100g of caster sugar and 25g of cocoa. Sprinkle this chocolate-sugar evenly over the chocolate sponge mixture. Pour 300ml of just-boiled water over the top and then pop the baking dish in the oven. Bake for 35–40 minutes, until set on top, then remove from the oven and leave to one side for 15 minutes. Sift over icing sugar and sprinkle with the reserved orange zest. Serve straight up, or with a dairy-free ice-cream, cream or yoghurt – whichever is your favourite!
