title: Phanouropita: the lost and found cake of Saint Phanourios
ingredients:
250ml light olive oil or other flavourless oil, plus extra for the tin
200g walnuts, plus extra, optional, for decorating
200g caster sugar
4 oranges or 1 orange and 250ml orange juice
300g self-raising flour
1 teaspoon baking powder
1 teaspoon ground cinnamon
100g raisins
125g icing sugar
steps:
Preheat your oven to 190°C/fan 170°C/gas mark 5. Grease a 24cm round cake tin with a little oil and line the base with greaseproof paper. Finely chop 75g of the walnuts and keep to one side. Grind the rest in a food processor or spice grinder until fine. In a large mixing bowl, whisk together the caster sugar with the oil until smooth. Finely grate in the zest of one orange. Squeeze all the oranges into a jug until you have 250ml juice, then whisk it into the oil and sugar mixture. Add the ground walnuts and sift in the self-raising flour, baking powder and ground cinnamon. Fold in the dry ingredients with a metal spoon, then stir in the raisins and chopped walnuts. Pour the batter into the prepared tin and bake for 40–45 minutes, or until cooked through. Cool in the tin for 10 minutes then transfer to a wire cooling rack.
Sift the icing sugar into a small mixing bowl and add just enough orange juice or water to make a thick but drizzle consistency icing – a couple of tablespoons should be enough. Drizzle over the cooled cake and decorate as you wish, with some grated orange zest, walnuts, candied orange peel or leave simply as is.

title: Helbeh: fenugreek cake
ingredients:
280g caster sugar
½ lemon
2 tablespoons orange blossom water, optional
15g fenugreek seeds
2 tablespoons tahini
350g fine semolina
100g plain flour
90ml olive oil
½ teaspoon aniseed
½ × 7g sachet of fast-action dried yeast
½ teaspoon baking powder
½ teaspoon ground cinnamon
½ teaspoon fine sea salt
40 blanched almonds, optional
steps:
Start by making the syrup. Place the caster sugar in a small pan with 375ml of water, the juice of the lemon half and the orange blossom water, if using. Bring to the boil over a high heat, then reduce the heat a little and leave to bubble away for about 8 minutes. You want this to be syrupy but not golden. When it is done, turn off the heat and leave to one side to cool completely. In another small pan, bring the fenugreek seeds to the boil in 500ml of water, and simmer over a medium heat until the water has reduced by about half. Leave this to cool completely also.
When the syrup and steeped fenugreek seeds are cold you can prepare the cake. Grease a 24cm round tin with the tahini. Whisk together the semolina and plain flour in a large mixing bowl. Add the olive oil and rub it into the dry ingredients until evenly mixed in, like breadcrumbs.
Grind the aniseed in a pestle and mortar and add to the mixing bowl along with the dried yeast, baking powder, ground cinnamon and fine sea salt. Stir everything together. Strain the cooked fenugreek seeds, reserving the liquid. Add the seeds to the bowl, along with 225ml of the cooking water. Mix it all together. Don’t overmix it, you just want it to come together – add one or two tablespoons more of the water if needed. Pat the dough into the greased tin and cut into diamonds – if you do about 40, this should make the pieces a good size. Pop an almond into each diamond, if using. Leave to one side for 1 hour, to prove a little.
Preheat your oven to 200°C/fan 180°C/gas mark 6. Bake the cake for 30–35 minutes, until golden. As soon as it is ready, evenly pour over the cooled syrup and leave the helbeh to cool. Do not cut this for at least 1 hour, but the longer you can leave it (overnight if possible), the better.

title: Hareeseh: Jordanian coconut semolina cake
ingredients:
340g caster sugar
½ lemon
1 tablespoon orange blossom water
1 tablespoon rose water
125ml vegetable or light olive oil, plus extra for the tin
300g regular semolina
50g desiccated coconut
½ tablespoon baking powder
200g dairy-free coconut yoghurt
30 almonds, to decorate
steps:
Start by making the syrup, as this needs to be completely cold when the cake is ready. Place 225g of the caster sugar in a small pan with 350ml of water and the juice from the lemon half. Bring to the boil over a medium heat, then reduce the heat a little and simmer for 10 minutes. Stir in the orange blossom and rose water and leave to one side to cool completely.
Preheat your oven to 200°C/fan 180°C/gas mark 6. Brush a 23 × 33cm roasting tin or 30–31cm circular tin with a little olive oil. In a large bowl, mix together the semolina, desiccated coconut, baking powder and the remaining 115g of caster sugar. Whisk together, then make a well and pour in the vegetable or olive oil. Mix it in with a fork so that every grain gets coated in oil, then mix in the coconut yoghurt. Mix together until combined – it will be a thick mixture. Spoon the mixture into the greased tin (you don’t want it to be more than 2.5cm thick) and gently score the top into small diamond shapes, about 3–4cm. Place a blanched almond into the centre of each piece and place the tin in the oven. Bake for 40–45 minutes, or until the top is golden brown.
When the cake comes out of the oven, slowly and evenly pour over the cooled syrup. Leave to soak in for at least 2 hours before serving.

title: Ghapama loaf cake
ingredients:
100g dairy-free spread, plus a little extra for the tin
100g raisins, dried apple or apricots, or a mixture
275g light soft brown sugar
75ml orange or apple juice
150g pumpkin purée, homemade or tinned
2 tablespoons honey (or maple syrup)
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
165g plain flour
2 teaspoons baking powder
1½ teaspoons ground cinnamon
¼ teaspoon ground cloves
¼ teaspoon salt
30g nuts (I like to use almonds, pistachios, walnuts)
Gold leaf, for decorating, optional
steps:
Grease and line a large loaf tin with greaseproof paper. If using dried apple or apricots, chop them into small pieces, around 1–2cm. Place all the dried fruit into a pan with 75g of the light soft brown sugar, 25g of the dairy-free spread and all the juice. Bring to a boil over a medium heat. Swirl the pan to help melt the sugar, then reduce the heat a little and leave to bubble gently away for 6–8 minutes, swirling the pan a few more times. When you have a thick, deep-golden syrup, remove the pan from the heat. Pour the syrup and fruit into the bottom of the lined loaf tin and leave to one side.
Preheat your oven to 190°C/fan 170°C/gas mark 5. Melt the remaining 75g of dairy-free spread. Place it in a large mixing bowl with the remaining 200g of light soft brown sugar and the pumpkin purée, honey and vanilla extract. Stir in four tablespoons of water and mix until smooth. Sift in the flour, baking powder, spices and salt, then fold into the wet mixture. When everything has just come together, spoon the batter into the lined tin and pop in the oven. Bake for 40–50 minutes, until golden and cooked through. Leave the cake in the tin to cool for 5 minutes before turning out onto a cooling rack. Chop the nuts and scatter over the cake. Leave to cool completely, then decorate with the gold leaf, if you like, and serve.

title: Pivčići: apricot, beer and walnut rolls
ingredients:
250g self-raising flour, plus extra for dusting
1½ teaspoons baking powder
A pinch of salt
100ml sunflower oil
100ml beer
60g apricot jam
150g caster sugar
½ lemon
100g walnuts
steps:
Preheat your oven to 190°C/fan 170°C/gas mark 5. In a mixing bowl, whisk together the self-raising flour, baking powder and salt and make a well in the centre. Pour in the sunflower oil and beer and whisk until a dough is formed. Knead for a minute then turn out onto a lightly floured surface. Divide the dough equally in two and roll each piece into a ball. Place the balls of dough between sheets of greaseproof paper and roll out into circles that are 2mm thick – it is important that they are circular. Cut each circle in half, then quarters and so on, until you have 16 triangles (32 in total). Spoon a small amount of jam onto the wide end of each triangle and start rolling the little rolls, from wide end in. Line baking trays with greaseproof paper – you can use the sheets you used to roll the dough – and evenly space out the little rolls. Pop the trays in the oven and bake for 15–18 minutes, swapping the trays part-way through if they’re cooking unevenly. When the rolls are done, they should be just golden.
While the rolls are baking, make the syrup. Place the sugar in a medium saucepan with 100ml of water and the juice from the lemon half. Bring to the boil, reduce the heat to low and simmer for 5 minutes. Grind the walnuts using a spice grinder or pestle and mortar – avoid using a food processor, if possible, as a bit of texture is needed here, and the walnuts go oily if they break down too much.
When the rolls are baked, pop them straight in the pan with the syrup. Do this in batches. Use tongs to turn them, and leave them in for less than a minute. You want them syrupy enough that the nuts stick , but not so soaked as to be soggy. Use the tongs to retrieve them from the syrup, roll in the ground walnuts and place on a tray. Keep going until all the biscuits are coated. Leave until cool before eating, and store any left over in an airtight container.

title: Melomakarona: spiced honey biscuits
ingredients:
500g plain flour, plus a little extra, if needed
1 teaspoon baking powder
½ teaspoon bicarbonate of soda
2 teaspoons ground cinnamon
1 teaspoon mixed spice
½ teaspoon fine sea salt
250g caster sugar
235ml olive oil
100ml orange juice
2 tablespoons brandy
150ml honey, plus extra for drizzling
1 cinnamon stick
75g walnuts
steps:
Preheat the oven to 180°C/fan 160°C/gas mark 4. Line two baking sheets with greaseproof paper. Sift the flour into a large mixing bowl, along with the baking powder, bicarbonate of soda, ground cinnamon, mixed spice and salt, then add 100g of the sugar. Make a well in the middle of the dry ingredients and pour in the olive oil, orange juice and brandy. Mix it all together, initially with a fork, then with your hands until it is combined and smooth. If the mixture feels a little greasy, add a little more flour, but only just enough to bring it together; it shouldn’t be too stiff.
Roll the dough into golf ball-sized pieces, and shape them slightly into an oblong shape. Space them out evenly on the lined baking sheets and place in the oven. Bake for 20–25 minutes, until golden.
Meanwhile, make the syrup. Place the honey in a small pan with the remaining 150g of caster sugar, 400ml of water and the cinnamon stick. Bring to the boil over a medium heat, then reduce to a simmer and leave to gently bubble for 6–8 minutes, until thickened. Finely chop the walnuts and keep to one side.
When the biscuits are ready, leave to cool for 10 minutes, then carefully dip each one into the warm honey syrup until completely coated. I do about four at a time and leave them in for about 30 seconds on each side. You don’t want to do too many at once, because you don’t want them to go soggy. Transfer the dipped melomakarona to a board, drizzle with a tiny bit more honey and sprinkle with the chopped walnuts. Leave to cool before serving, or store in an airtight container where they should keep nicely for at least a week.

title: Tahinobiskoto: tahini, almond and honey cookies
ingredients:
150g ground almonds
1 teaspoon baking powder
¼ teaspoon fine sea salt
100g tahini
90g honey
15g sesame seeds, a mixture of black and white, ideally
steps: Preheat your oven to 180°C/fan 160°C/gas mark 4. Line two baking sheets with greaseproof paper. Whisk together the ground almonds, baking powder and sea salt. Add the tahini and honey and beat together until smooth. Place the sesame seeds in a bowl or on a small plate. Divide the mixture into 12 and roll into balls in your hand. Roll each ball lightly in the sesame seeds and place on the lined baking sheet. Leave a good few centimetres between them as they can spread. Press down a little on each ball to flatten slightly. Bake in the oven for 8–10 minutes, or until the biscuits are lightly golden around the edge. Leave to cool on the tray for 5 minutes then transfer to a cooling rack.

title: Moustokouloura: spiced grape, honey and chocolate biscuits
ingredients:
500g plain flour
1 teaspoon baking powder
1 teaspoon bicarbonate of soda
1 tablespoon ground cinnamon
¼ teaspoon ground cloves
¼ teaspoon fine sea salt
175ml petimezi (grape molasses)
125ml light olive or vegetable oil, plus extra for greasing
5 tablespoons honey
2 tablespoons orange juice
150g dark chocolate
50g toasted sesame seeds or hazelnuts
Flaky sea salt
steps:
In a large mixing bowl whisk together the plain flour, baking powder, bicarbonate of soda, ground cinnamon, ground cloves and fine salt and leave to one side. In the bowl of a free-standing mixer, using a beater attachment, mix together the petimezi, oil, honey and orange juice. When the liquids are completely combined, add half the dry ingredients and combine using the beater attachment (you can also do this by hand). Add the remaining flour mixture, and mix together just enough to bring it together. Turn it out onto a lightly oiled worktop, and leave to rest for 30 minutes.
Preheat your oven to 190°C/fan 170°C/gas mark 5 and line two baking sheets with greaseproof paper. Divine the dough in half, then half again. Split each quarter into nine or 10 small balls. Roll a ball of dough into a sausage about 12cm long, then join the ends to form a circle or roll into a swirl, then place on a lined baking sheet. Continue with all the dough. Bake for about 13–15 minutes, or until just lightly golden, then leave to cool on the trays for 10 minutes, before transferring to a cooling rack.
When the biscuits have cooled, break up the chocolate into small, even pieces and melt in the microwave or in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of simmering water. Stir until glossy and smooth. Place the toasted sesame seeds in a bowl (if using hazelnuts, chop them very finely first). Half dip a biscuit into the melted chocolate then sprinkle with the sesame seeds or chopped hazelnuts and a little pinch of flaky sea salt. Transfer to a cooling rack to set, then repeat with all of the biscuits.

title: Mama’s halva
ingredients:
600ml almond milk
360g caster sugar
2 tablespoons orange blossom water
5 cloves
2 cinnamon sticks
1 orange
200ml sunflower or other flavourless oil, plus extra for the tin
140g blanched almonds
400g semolina (not fine)
Ground cinnamon, for sprinkling
steps:
Place the almond milk in a medium pan with 600ml of water, the caster sugar, orange blossom water, cloves and cinnamon sticks. Finely grate in the zest from the orange. Bring to the boil over a medium heat, then reduce the heat a little and simmer for 12–15 minutes, until lightly syrupy. Fish out the spices and set the syrup to one side.
Brush a medium bundt tin with a little oil. Chop the almonds, not too finely. Place the oil in a large pan over a medium-low heat. Warm it through for a minute then stir in the semolina. Toast the semolina for 5 minutes, until it turns golden – don’t let it get too dark or it will become bitter. Stir in the chopped almonds and gradually add the spiced syrup to the semolina. Keep stirring and when the syrup is all in, reduce the heat to low. As soon as the mixture starts bubbling, pour it into the greased tin. Chill in the fridge overnight to set. When you’re ready to serve the halva, cover the bundt tin with a large plate or platter and invert to turn out, then sprinkle liberally with ground cinnamon.

title: Pistachio and cardamom halva
ingredients:
Olive oil
50g pistachios
8 cardamom pods
250g tahini
½ teaspoon good-quality vanilla extract
½ teaspoon fine sea salt
230g caster sugar
steps:
Grease a loaf tin with a little oil then line it with cling film, leaving some overhanging the edges of the tin. Roughly chop the pistachios. Remove the cardamom seeds from the pods, discard the pods and grind the seeds until fine. Add to a large mixing bowl with 30g of the chopped pistachios, the tahini, vanilla and sea salt and beat until smooth.
Place the sugar and 75ml of water in a medium saucepan and gently bring to the boil over a medium heat. Gently swirl the pan, do not stir the syrup or the sugar will crystallise. Once it starts to bubble, reduce the heat to low and leave to simmer for around 12–15 minutes, until you have a thick syrup. If you have a sugar thermometer, it needs to reach 121°C. When it is ready, add the tahini mixture to the pan (you don’t want the mixture to cool down, it needs to stay in the warm pan) and quickly beat the two elements together to make a smooth paste. This is best done with a wooden spoon or spatula. Try not to overwork it, though, as this will make the halva crumbly – you only want to beat it for 30 seconds. As soon as it is smoothly combined, spoon it into the lined tin and press on the remaining pistachios. Leave to cool. Once cool, cover with the cling film edges and transfer to the fridge to set overnight before serving.

title: Mahalepi and mahalabia
ingredients:
7 tablespoons niseste or cornflour
3 tablespoons caster sugar, plus extra to serve
3 tablespoons rose water, plus extra to serve
Ice cubes
7 tablespoons cornflour
1 litre almond milk
275g caster sugar
1 tablespoon orange blossom water
½ lemon
1 tablespoon rose water
40g pistachios
25g flaked almonds
steps:
Mix enough water into the niseste (or cornflour) to make it into a loose paste – a few tablespoons should do it. Mix in three tablespoons of caster sugar and the rose water and leave to one side. In a medium saucepan, bring 1 litre of water to a simmer over a medium heat and pour in the rosewater paste. Whisk until it starts to bubble, then reduce the heat a little and cook for about 5 minutes, until you have a thick mixture. Rinse six small bowls under a cold tap and leave to one side; it’s important to keep them wet. When you’re happy that your mixture is smooth and thickened, pour into your bowls and leave to cool. As soon as they have cooled down, transfer to the fridge and leave to set overnight.
Once the mahalepi has set firm add a few tablespoons of cold water to each bowl, to keep the puddings from drying out. Alternatively, slide the round puddings into one larger dish, and cover with lots of cold water. They last happily in there, and take up less room in the fridge. Serve the mahalepi in bowls, roughtly diced and topped with a ladle of the chilled water, a tablespoon or so of caster sugar, an extra teaspoon of rose water, and a good spoonful of triantaphyllo drizzled on top. If it is really warm outside, add a couple of extra ice cubes.
Place the cornflour in a mixing bowl and whisk in enough almond milk to make a smooth paste. Pour the remaining milk into a large saucepan with 75g of the caster sugar and warm over a medium heat. When it starts to bubble, whisk in the cornflour mixture, and keep whisking. Lower the heat and cook over a lower heat for around 5–8 minutes, still whisking, until thickened and glossy. Stir in the orange blossom water and then pour or ladle into 6–8 serving bowls. Leave to cool then transfer to the fridge to set.
Meanwhile, make the syrup. Place the remaining 200g of caster sugar in a pan with 250ml of water and the juice from the lemon half. Bring to the boil over a high heat, then reduce to a simmer and leave to bubble away for 8–10 minutes until lightly syrupy but not golden. Stir in the rose water and leave to cool, then transfer to a jug.
When you are ready to serve, roughly chop the pistachios and decorate the puddings with the chopped and flaked nuts. Serve with the jug syrup on the side, for people to pour over according to their taste.

title: Erene’s rizogalo: rose rice pudding with roasted strawberries
ingredients:
750ml non-dairy milk, ideally coconut
160g pudding rice
150g granulated sugar
2 tablespoons rose water
1 tablespoon vanilla extract
250ml non-dairy cream
½–1 teaspoon ground cinnamon
300g strawberries
½ lemon
steps:
Place the milk and rice in a large heavy-bottomed saucepan, then add 100g granulated sugar, one tablespoon of rose water and half the vanilla extract. Bring to the boil over a medium heat, give it a good stir, then reduce the heat to low and cook for 25–30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the rice is perfectly cooked – just tender and creamy. Stir in the cream, warming through for 1 minute, then remove from the heat. Ladle into serving bowls, or one large bowl, and sprinkle liberally with the ground cinnamon. You can serve this now, or leave it to cool and then chill in the fridge, as is traditional.
For the strawberries, preheat your oven to 220°C/fan 200°C/gas mark 7. Hull the strawberries and halve any larger ones. Place the berries in a snug fitting roasting tray and toss with the remaining 50g of granulated sugar. Squeeze over the lemon juice, and add the remaining one tablespoon of rose water and half a tablespoon of vanilla extract. Mix together well and place the tray in the oven. Roast for 15–20 minutes, until the strawberries are tender but not mushy. Like the rizogalo, the strawberries are lovely served warm or chilled, just spoon them (and some of the juices from the tray) over a bowl of the creamy pudding.

title: Anthous: deep-fried flowers, honey and pistachio
ingredients:
2 pinches of fine sea salt
½ teaspoon fennel seeds
130g plain flour
1 teaspoon caster sugar
¼ teaspoon fast-action dried yeast
300ml cold sparkling water
1 litre vegetable oil
20g pistachios
12 courgette flowers or elderflower heads
3 tablespoons honey (agave or maple syrup will work well here)
steps:
Place a pinch of salt and the fennel seeds in a mortar and grind with the pestle until you have a fine powder. Place into a large bowl with the plain flour, caster sugar and dried yeast and whisk to combine. Slowly whisk in the sparkling water, until smooth, adding a splash more water if needed to reach a double-cream consistency. Then whisk in another pinch of salt. Cover the bowl with a tea towel and leave to one side.
Place the vegetable oil in a large saucepan on a medium heat. Place a small cube of bread or potato in the oil; when it turns golden-brown the oil is ready. Meanwhile, finely chop the pistachios. Trim the flowers, removing the stamen if using courgette flowers. Then when the oil is ready and you are ready to fry, dip the flowers in the batter, let the excess drip off, then carefully lower into the hot oil. You may need to do this in batches. Fry the flowers for 1–2 minutes, until golden and crisp, then transfer to a plate lined with kitchen paper to absorb any excess oil. Drizzle the hot fritters with honey, scatter with the chopped pistachios and serve immediately.

title: Ekmek: kataifi milk pie
ingredients:
375g caster sugar
1 cinnamon stick
3 cloves
5 tablespoons light olive or vegetable oil
200g kataifi pastry
10 tbsp cornflour
1.25 litres almond milk
2 tablespoons orange blossom water
2 tablespoons rose water
40g nuts, I like pistachio and almonds
Rose petals and gold leaf, optional, to decorate
steps:
Start by making the syrup so it has time to cool. Place 250g of the caster sugar in a small pan with 300ml of water, the cinnamon stick and cloves, and bring to the boil over a high heat. Once bubbling, reduce to a medium heat and leave to gently bubble away for around 6–8 minutes, until syrupy but not coloured. Leave to one side to cool completely. When cool, preheat your oven to 200°C/fan 180°C/gas mark 6. Brush a 24cm square cake tin with a little oil. Tease the kataifi into the bottom of the tin, then drizzle over the oil. Toss it through the pastry, then spread out the kataifi so it evenly covers the base. Bake in the oven for 20–25 minutes, or until evenly golden. Remove from the oven and evenly pour the cooled sugar syrup all over the pastry, discarding the spices. Leave to one side to cool.
When the pastry is cool, make the milk layer. Place the cornflour in a large mixing bowl and whisk in just enough of the almond milk to form a smooth paste – six tablespoons should be enough. Place the remaining almond milk and 125g caster sugar in a large pan and gently bring to the boil over a medium heat. Ladle a little hot milk into the cornflour mixture, whisk it in till smooth, then pour the cornflour-milk mixture into the pan with the rest of the milk and whisk together until well combined. Keep whisking over the heat until you feel the milk thicken, then reduce the heat a little, and add the orange blossom and rose waters. Keep whisking until you have a smooth custard that thickly coats the back of a spoon – this should take about 4–5 minutes. Pour the fragrant custard over the soaked and cooled kataifi pastry. Then it’s time to decorate. Roughly chop the nuts and scatter them over, along with some rose petals. I even like to add a little gold leaf once the custard has cooled. Once the ekmek has cooled completely, transfer it to the fridge for at least 4 hours, to allow it to set before serving.

title: Roasted cherry and tarragon hand pies
ingredients:
500g strong white bread flour, plus extra for dusting
¾ teaspoon fine sea salt
½ × 7g sachet of fast-action dried yeast
1 tablespoon caster sugar
450g cherries (or 400g frozen cherries)
3 tablespoons granulated sugar
1 tablespoon cornflour
1 lemon
2 tarragon sprigs
500ml vegetable oil, plus extra for greasing
150g icing sugar
steps:
Place the strong white bread flour in a large mixing bowl (or the bowl of a free-standing mixer) and whisk in the sea salt. In a jug, mix together the yeast, caster sugar and 250ml of warm water. Leave for a few minutes. Mix the yeast water into the flour, adding a few more tablespoons of water if the dough needs it to come together – it shouldn’t be dry. Knead the dough for 8–10 minutes, until smooth and elastic. Alternatively, use the free-standing mixer with a dough hook. Transfer to a clean, lightly oiled bowl and leave to prove for 1 hour.
Preheat your oven to 220°C/fan 200°C/gas mark 7. Destone the cherries (if using fresh), and if using frozen, take them out of the freezer 15 minutes before using. Place the cherries in a roasting tray just big enough to hold them in one layer. Sprinkle over the granulated sugar and cornflour. Halve the lemon and squeeze over most of the juice. Toss everything together then place the tray in the oven and roast for 15–20 minutes (depending on whether using fresh or frozen cherries). They should be slightly caramelised, and the juices surrounding them should be sticky and jammy. Remove from the oven and leave to one side to cool. Once cool, pick the tarragon leaves, finely chop and stir through.
As soon as everything is ready, turn the dough onto a lightly floured worktop and knead. Roll into a long even sausage and cut into 12 equal pieces. Roll each piece of dough into a ball. Take a piece of dough, flatten it into a circle in the palm of your hand about 5mm thick, and place a tablespoon of the roasted cherry mixture in the middle, then fold the dough over, so you have a semi-circle. Seal the edges by gently crimping and pressing them together.
When the pies are all ready, pour enough oil into a large frying or saucepan to come 3cm up the sides. Place on a medium heat. The oil is ready when you put a little dough in there and it starts to bubble and turn golden. Gently lower in three or four pies, and fry for 4–5 minutes. When they are golden brown, turn them over and cook for 2–3 minutes more. Transfer to a tray lined with kitchen paper and continue to fry until all the pies are cooked.
Sift the icing sugar into a mixing bowl and squeeze in enough of the remaining lemon juice until you get a thick, but runny icing (you may need a little water too). After 5 minutes, drizzle over the pies, then serve warm or at room temperature.

title: Shiamishi: fried orange-blossom custard pies
ingredients:
1 litre vegetable oil, plus extra for the tray
200g caster sugar
2 pieces of mastic , optional
160g fine semolina
1 tablespoon orange blossom water
500g plain flour
½ teaspoon fine sea salt
½ teaspoon baking powder
150ml olive oil
250g icing sugar
2 teaspoons ground cinnamon
steps:
Grease a 30 × 25cm baking or roasting tray with a little oil and set to one side. Pour 1.2 litres of water into a saucepan, stir in the caster sugar and place on a medium heat. Grind the mastic with a little extra caster sugar in a pestle and mortar until fine, and add to the pan. When the water is hot, but not boiling, pour the semolina in a slow, steady stream, whisking constantly. Add the orange blossom and keep whisking until it starts to bubble. It should be thick within a few minutes. When it is ready, spoon it into the greased tray and leave it to one side to cool – the custard should be around 1.5cm thick.
While it is cooling, make the dough. Place the flour in a large mixing bowl and whisk in the salt and baking powder. Make a well in the middle and pour in the olive oil. Use your fingers to rub the oil into the flour, then slowly pour in 200ml of tepid water. Bring the dough together, adding more water if necessary – you may need an extra one or two tablespoons. You want the dough to be on the slightly sticky side, rather than too dry. Knead it until smooth, then leave it to rest in a clean bowl, covered with a tea towel, for 30 minutes.
The next bit sounds fiddly but once you get in a rhythm it’s not too bad – it’s meditative, even. Clear your worktop, have a bowl with olive oil at the ready and grease a large baking tray. Slice the set semolina into 24 squares, so in a grid of four by six. Cut the dough into four, for ease. Take one of the pieces and divide into six small balls. Roll one of the balls into a rough square or circle, around 18cm big, as thin as you can. Then place one of the semolina squares in the middle and fold each side over the semolina, like an envelope. There should be pastry all around the custard square also, like a lip all the way around. Once it is all enclosed, place on a lightly floured tray and keep going until all the pastry and all the semolina is used.
When the shiamishi parcels are all ready, place the oil in a large pan on a medium heat and bring to 160°C. If you put a piece of bread, or even dough, in the oil, you will know it is ready when it starts to sizzle and turn golden. In batches, so as not to overcrowd the pan, gently lower the parcels into the oil and fry for around 3 minutes on each side, until golden all over. Remove with a slotted spoon onto a piece of kitchen paper, then serve immediately, dusted with the icing sugar mixed with the cinnamon. Keep frying until they are all cooked and eat while still hot.

title: Anoush abour: Christmas barley pudding, the oldest dessert in the world
ingredients:
250g pearl barley
1 cinnamon stick
150g dried apricots
150g golden raisins
1 teaspoon ground cinnamon
¼ teaspoon ground cloves
½ teaspoon fennel seeds
250g blanched nuts – walnuts, almonds, pistachios and pine nuts
200g honey
1 pomegranate
2 tablespoons rose water
Hundreds and thousands, edible rose petals or candied fennel seeds, optional
steps:
Start preparing the day before you want to serve the anoush abour. Place the pearl barley in a large bowl and cover with plenty of cold water. Leave to one side for 2 hours. Drain and place in a large pan with the cinnamon stick and 2.5 litres of water. Bring to the boil over a high heat, then reduce to a low heat, cover and simmer for 1½ hours. Remove from the heat. Leave to one side to cool, adding more water if it has almost completely been absorbed. Boil a kettle. Finely chop the dried apricots and place in a small pan with the raisins and cover with 300ml of just-boiled water. Stir in the ground cinnamon and ground cloves. Lightly crush the fennel seeds and stir them in, too. Cover and leave both pans overnight.
The next day, chop 150g of the mixed nuts and add to the pan with the dried fruit along with the honey. If your fruit has entirely absorbed the liquid, you may want to add a couple of tablespoons of water. Bring to a simmer over a medium heat, then cook for 5–8 minutes, until there is no liquid left in the pan, or only a very reduced amount. Stir into the cooked pearl barley and place the large pan on a low heat to warm through for around 15 minutes. While it is on the hob, pick the pomegranate seeds. When the pudding is ready, stir in the rose water and serve the anoush abour warm, or at room temperature. Garnish with the remaining nuts and pomegranate seeds, and hundreds and thousands or candied fennel seeds, if using.

title: Rose petal jam
ingredients:
250g organic edible rose petals (see introduction)
1kg jam sugar
1 lemon
5 tablespoons liquid pectin
100g organic edible rose petals (see introduction)
500g granulated sugar
1 lemon
steps:
Place a saucer or side plate in the freezer and sterilise your jars ready for storing the jam. You can do this by washing the jars thoroughly, then drying out in the oven for 15 minutes at 120°C/fan 100°C/gas mark ½. Once they come out of the oven be careful not to touch the inside or you’ll need to repeat the process to make them sterile again.
Gently wash the rose petals and place them in a large, heavy-bottomed saucepan or flameproof casserole. Stir in the jam sugar and 200ml of water. Place on a medium-low heat and stir gently until the sugar has dissolved. Once it is no longer grainy, squeeze in the lemon juice, turn the heat up just a little and cook for around 10 minutes, until it starts to thicken. To test the jam, spoon a tiny bit on to one of the plates from your freezer and push your finger through it. If it starts to wrinkle and crease then the jam is ready. If it stays runny then you need to return the plate to the freezer and cook the jam for a further 5–10 minutes. Keep testing the jam on the cold plate until you get to the desired consistency. Turn off the heat and leave to cool for 10 minutes, then spoon the jam into the sterilised jars and seal. It will keep this way for a few months.
For triantaphyllo: If you want to make triantaphyllo (rose syrup) then simply place the rose petals in 500ml of water and add the granulated sugar. Gently bring to the boil then simmer on a medium heat for 10 minutes. Add the juice of the lemon, and simmer for 5 more minutes. Then cool, strain and transfer to sterilised bottles (see here ). This will keep for a few months; once opened, store in the fridge.

title: Roasted apricot compote
ingredients:
800g apricots
400g granulated sugar
3 tablespoons water
1 lemon
2 tablespoons orange blossom water, optional
steps:
Preheat your oven to 180°C/fan 160°C/gas mark 4. Halve the apricots, remove the stones, and cut any large cheeks in half again. Place the fruit in a large roasting tin, and add the granulated sugar and three tablespoons of water. Squeeze in the juice of the lemon and add the orange blossom water, if using. Mix together and leave to one side for 10 minutes. Meanwhile, carefully crack open three of the apricot stones (use a nut cracker if you have one, or place them in a sandwich bag and crack with a rolling pin) and take out the kernel from the centre of the stone. Place the three kernels into the tray, and stir in, then set the tray aside. After 10 minutes, transfer the tray to the oven and bake for 1 hour, stirring every 20 minutes or so, crushing with the back of a fork until the apricots are sticky and cooked down, and just a little golden around the edges. Remember it will thicken as it cools, so don’t worry if it is a little on the liquid side at this stage.
If you want to store this for the future, transfer to sterilised jars while still hot, and seal (see here ). It will now keep for a few months. Otherwise, leave to cool, then transfer to airtight containers and keep in the fridge for a few weeks.

title: Pumpkin and geranium preserve
ingredients:
1kg pumpkin
2 oranges
1 lemon
800g granulated sugar
2 scented geranium leaves
steps: Cut the pumpkin in half and scoop out the seeds. Cut in half again and peel the quarters. If you have a food processor with a coarse grating attachment then use that to grate the flesh. Otherwise finely chop the flesh using a large, sharp knife. Place the pumpkin in a large, heavy-bottomed saucepan. Finely grate in the zest of the oranges and lemon. Squeeze the juice from all the fruit into a measuring jug and top with enough water so you have 300ml. Pour this into the pan and stir in along with the sugar and geranium leaves. Place the pan on a high heat, bring to the boil then reduce the heat to low and simmer for 4–8 minutes until the pumpkin is just tender. The time will depend on whether you grated or finely chopped it; carefully taste a bit to see how it yields – you want it to be turning tender. Turn the heat up to a boil again and cook rapidly for 15–20 minutes, stirring often, until the jam is sticky, glossy and thickened, and the liquid has almost completely reduced. Once it is ready, transfer to sterilised jars and seal while still hot. Alternatively, leave to cool, and store in airtight containers in the fridge for a few weeks.

title: Date and cardamom butter
ingredients:
200g medjool dates
2 oranges
5 cardamom pods
½ teaspoon fine sea salt
Pistachio and edible rose petals, to garnish, optional
steps: Halve the dates, remove and discard the stones and place the fruit in a small saucepan. Squeeze over the juice of both the oranges and top with enough water to just cover the fruit. Bring to the boil over a medium heat. Once boiling, reduce the heat to low and simmer for 20 minutes, until the dates are tender. Meanwhile, remove the seeds from the cardamom pods (discarding the pods), and finely grind using a pestle and mortar. Place the softened dates into a food processor with the crushed cardamom seeds and the salt. Blitz to a smooth paste – add a couple of tablespoons of the cooking liquid to help the paste get going, if needed. If the spread feels a little on the loose side, return the blended mixture back to the pan and cook over a low heat for 5 minutes until thickened and dried out a little. Spoon the paste onto a serving dish and garnish with chopped pistachios and rose petals, if you like.

title: Sykomaitha: fig, anise and almond wheel
ingredients:
10 fig leaves
250g dried figs
4 tablespoons ouzo, mastiha liqueur or zivania (see here )
40g almonds or walnuts
2 fennel herb fronds (if you can get it)
3 black peppercorns
¼ teaspoon aniseed
¼ teaspoon ground cinnamon
1 tablespoon caster sugar, optional
5 tablespoons petimezi (grape molasses) or honey
Olive oil
steps:
Soak the fig leaves in a large bowl of cold water. Finely chop the dried figs (discarding the stalk ends) and place in a large bowl. Stir in the ouzo, mastiha liqueur or zivania and leave to one side for 30 minutes. Chop the almonds or walnuts – I like a mixture of very fine and slightly larger pieces. Finely chop the fennel herb, if using. Use a spice mill or pestle and mortar to grind the black peppercorns and aniseed until fine.
Preheat your oven to 140°C/fan 120°C/gas mark 1. When the chopped figs are ready, add the chopped nuts, fennel and all the ground spices to the bowl. Mix together well and knead with your hands until you have a smooth paste. Taste a little bit and if it is a tad bitter, knead in the sugar until well combined.
I find it easier and less messy to make the wheels in conveyor-belt fashion. Lay five of the soaked fig leaves out in front of you. Divide the fig mixture equally into five, roll into balls and place each in the centre of a leaf. Flatten each ball down with the palm of your hand. Brush each fig patty with the grape must or honey, turning over and brushing the other side too, then top with one of the remaining fig leaves. Tuck in the edges of the leaves, and tie each wheel up with string, so that the mixture inside is completely encased. Oil a large baking sheet. Place the wheels on the baking sheet bake for about 2 hours, so that they are golden on the outside and intense and dried out in the middle. When you press on them, they should be firm, not squishy. Leave to cool before serving with cheese or as part of a meze.
If stored in an airtight container in a cool dark place, these sykomaitha will last for months in their leaves.

title: Glyko tou koutaliou: spoon sweets
ingredients:
4 lemons
2kg quince
1.4kg granulated sugar
3 scented geranium leaves
1kg small, green walnuts
2 tablespoons pickling lime, optional
3 lemons
1kg caster sugar
1 cinnamon stick
6 cloves
2 scented geranium leaves, optional
steps:
You will need some sterilised jars . Squeeze one of the lemons into a large pan of water. Peel the quince, cut into quarters and cut out the core. If they are small, leave them this size. If they are extraordinarily large (as some quince are), cut the wedges in half again, placing them in the lemon water as you go to stop them discolouring. When they are all prepared, place the pan on a high heat and bring to the boil. Boil for 20 minutes, then drain the quince and reserve the water. Place 1.2 litres of the cooking water back in the pan with the sugar and scented geranium leaves, and stir together. Squeeze in the juice of the remaining three lemons and bring to the boil over a medium heat. Boil for 15 minutes, then return the poached quince back to the pan. Reduce the heat a little and cook for a further 15–20 minutes, or until the syrup is thick, and the quince is tender. Spoon the hot fruit and syrup into sterilised jars, and seal while hot. Stored this way, placed in a dark cool cupboard, the unopened jars will keep for months.
Start by peeling and soaking the walnuts. Although my yiayia would do this with a paring knife, the easiest way is with a vegetable peeler. Either way, you need to wear gloves or the young walnuts will turn your hands black. You just want to peel off the dark green outer layer, as if peeling a carrot. Slice off the tops where they were attached to the tree, and prick the walnuts all over with the tip of the knife. Place in a large bowl of cold water for eight days, changing the water every day (even twice a day if you can).
Early in the morning on the eighth day (you’ll want to start this process as soon as you can), dissolve the lime in a large bowl of cold water and stir in the walnuts. Leave for 4 hours, or until the nuts feel hard. Drain and rinse them under running water to really rinse off the lime (skip this step if you aren’t using lime). Place the walnuts in a large pan of fresh water and bring to the boil. Boil for a couple of minutes, drain and repeat this boiling process twice more. On the third boil, reduce the heat and leave the walnuts to cook for 1–1½ hours, or until they are tender. You can check this by piercing a walnut on a skewer or sharp knife and seeing if it slides off. It should fall off easily. When they are ready, remove from the heat, drain and leave to cool.
Place the cooled walnuts in a bowl, cover with cold water and the juice from two of the lemons and leave for 1 hour. Drain the walnuts, then place in a large pan with the caster sugar, cinnamon, cloves, geranium leaves (if using) and just enough water to cover – about a litre. Bring to the boil over a medium-high heat, then reduce the heat a little and rapidly simmer until the syrup coats the back of a spoon. Skim off any scum that rises to the surface while boiling. When it is all ready, squeeze and stir in the juice of the final lemon, then spoon everything into sterilised jars . Seal and keep in a cool dark cupboard.

title: Ypovrichio: mastic spoon sweet
ingredients:
500g caster sugar
1 tablespoon lemon juice
½ teaspoon mastic pieces
¼ teaspoon vanilla extract
steps:
Sterilise some small jars .
Reserve one teaspoon of caster sugar, then place the rest in a heavy-bottomed pan with 300ml of water. Heat gently over a medium heat until the sugar is completely dissolved. Squeeze in half a tablespoon of lemon juice, then turn up the heat a little and bring to the boil. Leave it to bubble away for around 15 minutes until the mixture starts to thicken. To test if the glyko is ready, spoon a little of the thickened syrup into a glass of cold water. Use your fingers to see if it can form a little ball; if it isn’t quite at that stage, return the pan to the hob for a further 5 minutes, then try again. When the glyko is ready, place the pan in a sink filled with a couple of inches of cold water, and leave to cool completely.
Meanwhile, grind the mastic in a pestle and mortar with the reserved teaspoon of caster sugar until completely ground. When the glyko is completely cool, add a further half-tablespoon of lemon juice, the ground mastic and the vanilla extract. Beat it vigorously with a wooden spoon until thoroughly integrated, white and glossy. If the paste is a little too thick to beat, loosen it with a splash of water. When the glyko is ready, turn it out on to a clean, damp worktop and knead it until it feels rubbery. Pop the glyko into a sterilised jar, and seal. Unopened, this will keep for months, but once opened store in a cool dark spot or the fridge. Serve the jar of submarine with a glass of iced water. Take a teaspoon, scoop out a little of the glyko and dip into the water. It will help set it a little, like a lollipop. Refreshing, sweet and fun.

title: Russian priests, kvass and a plant-based diet
ingredients:
1 tablespoon honey
2g fast-action dried yeast
750ml purified water
A pinch of fine sea salt
225g raspberries or strawberries, hulled and roughly chopped
2 mint sprigs, leaves picked
200g rhubarb, sliced
2 thin slices of fresh ginger
1 apple core
3 pears, sliced
1 tablespoon raisins
steps:
Sterilise your jar and place your chosen fruit and flavouring inside. Mix the honey and yeast with a little of the water and add to the jar with the remaining water – you want to fill the jar but leave a 2cm gap between the contents and the lid. Add the salt, seal with the lid, give it a gentle shake to mix everything together then leave to one side. You want to give it a little shake a couple of times a day while it is fermenting.
After one or two days you should start to see the bubbles inside. When you do, release the lid and let out a little of the air. At this point you can leave the kvass for up to one week, depending on what fruits you are using and their sugar content. You are essentially aiming for fruit that looks like it has been poached or cooked with even more bubbles around it. If you are unsure, taste the liquid every day – this is the best way to check when it is ready. When it is to your liking, strain the kvass and discard the fruit. Bottle the kvass and pop it in the fridge – this will stop it fermenting further. However, if you want a more carbonated, fermented kvass, just leave it out of the fridge for a couple more days once it is strained and bottled.

title: Jallab
ingredients:
4 tablespoons date molasses
4 tablespoons grape molasses
2 tablespoons pomegranate molasses
2 teaspoons rose water
½ lemon
2 tablespoons pine nuts
2 tablespoons golden raisins
steps: Place the three kinds of molasses in a large jug. Add the rose water and squeeze in the lemon juice, discarding the pips. Top with 1 litre of cold water and stir well. Taste and add a little more water if you like. Decant into ice-filled glasses and garnish each drink with a teaspoon of pine nuts and a teaspoon of golden raisins.

title: Sharbat: mint and rose lemonade
ingredients:
4 lemons
4 tablespoons caster sugar
1 tablespoon rose water
3 mint sprigs
2 large handfuls of ice
steps: Finely grate the zest of two lemons (be careful not to get any of the white pith as this will make it bitter) and place in a blender with the juice from all four. Add the sugar, rose water, leaves from the mint sprigs and 350ml of water. Blitz on a high speed until smooth. Divide the ice and remaining mint leaves between four glasses and pour over the sharbat. Serve straight away.

title: Sbiten, uzvar: spiced honey drinks
ingredients:
150g blackberry jam
150g honey
2 cinnamon sticks
8 cloves
1 teaspoon ground ginger
150g dried apple
100g dried pear
50g dried prunes
50g dried cherries (or even dried dark mulberries if you have them)
1 cinnamon stick
Honey, to taste
steps:
Place all the ingredients with 1.2 litres of water in a large saucepan and slowly bring to the boil over a medium heat. Boil for 5 minutes, until the blackberry jam and honey have dissolved, then remove from the heat. Leave to cool to room temperature and strain out the spices. Transfer to a clean pan, bring to a simmer and serve hot. Otherwise, transfer to a sterilised bottle (see here ) and keep in the fridge to warm as needed (or drink cool).
Place all the dried fruit and the cinnamon stick in a large saucepan and cover with 2.5 litres of cold water. Leave for 1 hour then bring to the boil over a medium heat. Once boiling, reduce the heat to low and simmer for 30 minutes. Remove the pan from the heat, and leave to cool completely (ideally overnight). Once cool, strain the liquid and store in sterilised bottles in the fridge (see here ). Discard the cinnamon stick and keep the dried fruit to have for breakfast or pudding. Serve the uzvar cold or warm, with honey to sweeten as needed.

title: Dasogalo: spiced bread and almond milk
ingredients:
225g plain white bread (not sourdough)
100g blanched or ground almonds
2 pieces of mastic, or ½ tablespoon rose water
75g caster sugar
¼ teaspoon ground cinnamon
Nutmeg, to finish
steps: Remove and discard the crust from the bread and chop the rest into small cubes. Place in a large saucepan with the almonds and 1.5 litres of water. Grind the mastic, if using, with a little caster sugar using a pestle and mortar or spice grinder, then add it to the pan with the rest of the caster sugar. Place the pan on a medium heat and gently bring everything to the boil. Reduce the heat and simmer for 5 minutes. Blitz it all up with a stick blender until creamy and very smooth. Strain the mixture through a fine sieve into a jug and chill until needed. If you’re using rose water, stir it in now, a little at a time to taste. Serve the dasogalo over ice, finished with a sprinkle of ground cinnamon and fresh grating of nutmeg.

title: Grapefruit, orange and bergamot cordial
ingredients:
750g caster sugar
750ml freshly squeezed citrus juice – a couple of grapefruit and bergamot, topped up with orange, works well
steps: Place the caster sugar in a large saucepan and stir in 750ml of cold water. Pop on a medium heat and stir until the sugar has dissolved. Turn the heat up and bring to the boil, then reduce a little, just so that the mixture maintains a steady rolling boil without overflowing. Cook for 8 minutes, until syrupy but not golden or coloured at all. Pour the citrus juice into the pan, through a coarse sieve to catch any pips, and stir to combine. Reduce to a medium heat and simmer for 4–5 minutes. I don’t like to bring my cordial to the boil; I just heat it through enough to combine it well but not kill off all the vitamins. However, you will end up with a more concentrated cordial if you let it simmer, which is not a bad thing. Spoon off any scum that has risen to the surface, then leave the cordial to cool slightly. Meanwhile sterilise glass bottles and lids (see here ), as this will preserve your cordial for longer – you’ll be able to keep it unopened for months in the fridge. Use a funnel to pour the slightly cooled cordial into the bottles, then seal and leave to cool completely. Store in the fridge, then serve topped with ice and cold still or sparkling water for a refreshing drink.
